title: PostgreSQL
intro: What the database does with the SQL you write, and the exact places a plausible query returns a wrong answer without an error. Everything is run against PostgreSQL 16 in a container.

topics.title: What the Database Does
topics.intro: If you write SQL that works but have never looked at what the engine does with it, this is the layer underneath. Everything runs against PostgreSQL 16: the engine most likely to be under whatever you build next, and one of the few that will hand you a raw page and tell you what is on it. A container and a psql prompt is the whole setup.

topics.title: Queries That Look Right
topics.intro: SQL almost never fails loudly. A misplaced filter, a join that multiplies rows or an integer division does not throw an error. It returns a plausible, well-formatted, wrong answer, and that answer ends up in a dashboard or an invoice. These days take the fundamentals everyone believes they already know (the order a query runs in, what a LEFT JOIN promises, what ORDER BY guarantees, what a number or a timestamp really holds) and find the exact place where that belief and the engine disagree. Same setup as before: PostgreSQL 16 in a container and a psql prompt.

days.title: A table is a file of pages
days.teaser: Your UPDATE didn't update anything, and VACUUM gave back none of the 4 GB
days.teachBack: A page is the unit of I/O, and an UPDATE writes a new version of the row rather than editing it. Put those two facts together and explain why a table can triple in size while its row count stays flat, and what plain VACUUM does about it, given that it does not shrink the file.
days.theoryMarkdown:
You already write queries that work. This track is about the layer underneath them: what
the engine does with the bytes once your `SELECT` arrives. Start with the most physical
question there is: where does a row actually live?

Everything below is run against **PostgreSQL 16**, because it is the engine most likely
to be under whatever you build next, and because it is unusually willing to show you its
own internals. Stack Overflow's developer survey has had it as the most-used database
since 2023, and by 2025 it had pulled to 55.6% of all respondents (58.2% of professional
developers), roughly eighteen points clear of MySQL in second. It earns this track for a
different reason, though: you can ask Postgres to hand you a raw 8 kB page and tell you
what is on it, and almost nothing else will.

### A row is not the unit of anything

The mental model most people carry is that a table is a list of rows, and reading a row
reads a row. Neither half is true.

A table on disk is a flat array of fixed-size **pages**. Postgres calls the file a
*heap*. Every page is the same size, and the page is the unit the engine reads, writes,
caches and locks. Rows are packed into pages; a page holds as many as fit. When you ask
for one row, the engine reads the whole page that row sits in, because that is the
smallest thing it can read.

```sql
SHOW block_size;
```

```
 block_size
------------
 8192
```

8192 bytes, and it is a compile-time constant: changing it means rebuilding Postgres and
recreating every cluster, which is why essentially nobody does. SQLite defaults to 4096,
matching the virtual-memory page and most filesystem blocks. The number is a compromise
nobody has wanted to relitigate since the 1990s: bigger pages waste less space on
per-page bookkeeping and read more useful bytes per seek, while smaller pages waste less
I/O when you only wanted one row.

Watch the file grow in page-sized steps rather than row-sized ones:

```sql order
CREATE TABLE t(id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, name text, note text);
SELECT pg_relation_size('t') / 8192 AS pages;
INSERT INTO t(name, note) SELECT 'name' || g, repeat('x', 40) FROM generate_series(1, 2000) g;
SELECT pg_relation_size('t') / 8192 AS pages, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('t')) AS heap;
```

```
 pages
-------
     0

 pages |  heap
-------+--------
    23 | 184 kB
```

A freshly created Postgres table is **zero pages**, an empty file. (SQLite's answer is
different and worth knowing: creating a table there costs pages before any row exists,
because the schema and the table's own tree root have to live somewhere.) Then 2000 rows
land in 23 pages, and the file grew one page at a time at moments that had nothing to do
with your row count. Ninety-seven of those rows fit on the first page, and by the end of
this lesson you will be able to work that number out instead of guessing it.

### Where a row is, exactly

Every Postgres row carries hidden system columns you never declared. The one that
answers "where does this row live" is `ctid`:

```sql
SELECT ctid, id, name FROM t WHERE id IN (1, 2, 82) ORDER BY id;
```

```
  ctid  | id |  name
--------+----+--------
 (0,1)  |  1 | name1
 (0,2)  |  2 | name2
 (0,82) | 82 | name82
```

`(page, slot)`. Row 1 is the first slot of page zero; row 82 is the 82nd slot of the same
page. This is a **physical address**, and the next section shows that a row's address can
change while the row stays the same row.

### An UPDATE does not update

Update a row and ask for its address again:

```sql
UPDATE t SET note = 'changed' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT ctid FROM t WHERE id = 1;
```

```
  ctid
---------
 (22,56)
```

The row moved from page 0 to page 22. Postgres did not modify the row in place. It wrote
a **new version** of the row wherever there was space, and marked the old one as dead.
Both copies are in the file right now.

This is MVCC (multi-version concurrency control), the mechanism behind Postgres's
most-loved property: readers never block writers and writers never block
readers, because a reader is looking at a version that hasn't gone anywhere. The two
other hidden columns are the bookkeeping:

```sql
SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;
```

```
  ctid   | xmin | xmax | id
---------+------+------+----
 (22,56) |  798 |    0 |  1
 (0,2)   |  797 |    0 |  2
 (0,3)   |  797 |    0 |  3
```

`xmin` is the transaction that created this version, `xmax` the transaction that deleted
it (0 if it is still live). Row 1 wears its update on its sleeve: same table, same
`INSERT`, but a *newer* `xmin` than its neighbours, because the version you are looking
at was created by the `UPDATE` and not by the insert. Every query you run is really "show me the versions visible
to my transaction id", which is why a long-running `SELECT` can sit there returning a
consistent snapshot of a table being rewritten underneath it.

The bill arrives as **bloat**:

```sql order
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('t')) AS before_updates;
UPDATE t SET note = note || 'a';
SELECT count(*) AS live_rows, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('t')) AS file FROM t;
```

Run that middle statement three times, changing the appended character each time, so
every row gets three new versions:

```
 live_rows |  file
-----------+--------
      2000 | 720 kB
```

Same 2000 rows, and the file went from 184 kB to 720 kB. Three updates of every row left
three dead versions of every row lying in the heap. Now clean up:

```sql order
VACUUM t;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('t')) AS after_vacuum;
VACUUM FULL t;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('t')) AS after_vacuum_full;
```

```
 after_vacuum
--------------
 720 kB

 after_vacuum_full
-------------------
 184 kB
```

Plain `VACUUM` gave back nothing. It marks the dead space reusable *by that table*, so
the file stops growing, but it does not shrink the file, which surprises a lot of people
who run Postgres. `VACUUM FULL` does return the space, by rewriting the whole table into
a new file, and it takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for
the duration: nothing reads or writes that table until it finishes. On a large production
table that is an outage, which is why teams reach for `pg_repack` instead, and why "our
disk is full and `VACUUM` didn't help" is a support conversation that happens every week
of the year.

> [!NOTE]
> **The most expensive consequence of ctid, in production.** Because an index entry
> points at a physical `(page, slot)`, moving a row means every index on the table has to
> be updated, including indexes on columns your `UPDATE` never touched. Uber's engineering
> blog made this famous in 2016 as their headline reason for migrating off Postgres:
> a table with a dozen indexes turned a one-column update into twelve index writes, and
> that amplification then rode through their replication stream, which ships physical
> page changes rather than statements. MySQL's InnoDB avoids it by making secondary
> indexes point at the primary key instead of a physical location, which costs an extra
> lookup on every index read. Postgres pays on writes and InnoDB pays on reads.

### Worth knowing: ask Postgres for the raw bytes of a page

There is a contrib extension that reads pages directly, and it turns every claim above
into something you can check yourself. Rebuild the table first if you have been updating
it: the numbers below are page 0 of a table freshly loaded with those 2000 rows.

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT lower, upper, pagesize FROM page_header(get_raw_page('t', 0));
SELECT count(*) AS tuples, min(lp_len) AS small, max(lp_len) AS big FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('t', 0));
```

```
 lower | upper | pagesize
-------+-------+----------
   412 |   432 |     8192

 tuples | smallest | largest
--------+----------+---------
     97 |       79 |      80
```

Do the arithmetic and the page layout falls out of it. A page starts with a 24-byte
header, then grows an array of 4-byte **line pointers** downward from the front while the
row data itself is stacked upward from the back. `lower` is where the pointer array ends,
`upper` where the data begins, and the gap between them is the free space: here
432 − 412 = 20 bytes, so this page is full.

Which gives you an invariant to check rather than a number to believe:
**`lower` = 24 + 4 × tuples**. Here that is 24 + 97 × 4 = 412, exactly. Run those two
queries against any page of any table of your own and it will still hold, whatever the
counts happen to be. That layer of indirection is also why a row can be moved *within* a
page without any index noticing: the line pointer keeps the slot number stable while the
data behind it moves.

Now account for one row's 79 bytes. Eight for the bigint, six for `'name1'`, 41 for the
40-character note (varying-length values each carry a length byte), and the other 24 are
a per-row header that is yours whether you want it or not. Postgres charges 23 bytes of
visibility bookkeeping per row, rounded up for alignment. That is why a table of millions
of narrow rows is far bigger than `rows × columns` suggests, and why "just add a boolean
column" is never as free as it sounds.

> [!NOTE]
> **The clock nobody watches until it stops them.** Transaction ids are 32-bit, so they
> wrap. Postgres protects itself by refusing all writes once a table's oldest unfrozen
> transaction gets too far behind. `SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name =
> 'autovacuum_freeze_max_age'` shows the threshold, 200 million by default, against a
> 2^31 ceiling. Vacuum's *other* job, besides reclaiming space, is freezing old rows so
> this never happens. When it falls behind on a write-heavy table the ending is always
> the same: Sentry's engineering blog describes losing most of a US working day to
> exactly this, and the only recovery is to stop accepting writes and vacuum.

write.setup:
CREATE TABLE t(id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, name text, note text);
INSERT INTO t(name, note) SELECT 'name' || g, repeat('x', 40) FROM generate_series(1, 200) g;

challenges.prompt: Show where rows 1, 2 and 82 of `t` physically live: return the hidden location column (`ctid`) and `id`, in `id` order.
challenges.solution: SELECT ctid, id FROM t WHERE id IN (1, 2, 82) ORDER BY id;
challenges.hint: Every row carries a system column that says which page and slot it sits in.

challenges.prompt: Change the `note` of row 1 to `'changed'`, then return that row's location. It should be the *new* one: an UPDATE writes a new version of the row.
challenges.solution:
UPDATE t SET note = 'changed' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT ctid FROM t WHERE id = 1;
challenges.hint: Two statements. The second one is the same system column as before.

challenges.prompt: Return the size of the table's heap file as a human-readable string, the way `psql` would show it (like `640 kB`).
challenges.solution: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('t'));
challenges.hint: One function measures the relation in bytes, another one prettifies bytes.

quiz.prompt: A table has 200 rows packed into 6 pages. A query returns exactly one row, found by scanning. What is the smallest amount of data the engine could have read from disk?

options.text: One page: 8 kB in PostgreSQL
options.why: The page is the unit of I/O. Even a single-byte column in a single row costs one whole page, because a page is the smallest thing the engine can ask the filesystem for.

options.text: Just the bytes of that row
options.why: Nothing in the stack can read a partial page. The row's bytes arrive inside the page that holds them; you never pay per row.

options.text: All six pages, since a scan reads the whole table
options.why: A scan *may* read every page, but it can stop the moment it has what it needs. The question asks for the smallest possible, and that is the one page the row sits on.

options.text: It depends entirely on the row's width
options.why: Width changes how many rows fit per page, not the size of a read. A 20-byte row and a 2000-byte row both cost one page to reach.

quiz.prompt: You run `UPDATE t SET note = 'x' WHERE id = 1` in PostgreSQL. What happens to the row's physical location, and to the previous version of the row?

options.text: The row's bytes are overwritten where they sit, so the ctid is unchanged
options.why: That would break the property Postgres is built around: a concurrent reader holding an older snapshot must still be able to see the previous version. It cannot, if you overwrote it. The old version has to survive the update.

options.text: The old version is deleted immediately and the new one takes its slot
options.why: Immediate deletion has the same problem: a transaction that started before your update is entitled to keep reading the old version. Reclaiming that space is a *later*, separate job, which is exactly what VACUUM is for.

options.text: The row moves only if the new value is longer than the old one
options.why: Length is irrelevant to whether a new version is written; a new version is always written. It can influence *where* the new version lands, but even shrinking a value produces a second copy.

options.text: A new version of the row is written elsewhere, possibly on a different page, and the old version stays in the file, marked dead
options.why: This is MVCC. An UPDATE is an insert plus a tombstone, never an edit in place. Watch `ctid` change across the statement and you have seen it happen; the dead version is still on disk until a vacuum reclaims its space.

quiz.prompt: Your table's file is 4 GB on disk, of which only 500 MB is live rows. You run `VACUUM`. What happens to the size of the file, and why?

options.text: It stays 4 GB, and the dead space is permanently wasted until the table is dropped
options.why: Half right, and the wrong half matters. The space is not wasted: it is on the free space map and the next inserts and updates will land in it. That is why a well-vacuumed table reaches a steady size instead of growing forever.

options.text: It stays 4 GB: VACUUM marks the dead space reusable by that table but does not return it to the operating system
options.why: This is the most misunderstood thing in Postgres operations. Plain VACUUM stops the file from growing further, because new rows fill the freed space, but the file only shrinks if free space happens to sit at the very end. To actually get the 3.5 GB back you need VACUUM FULL, which rewrites the table into a new file under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, or pg_repack, which does it without the lock.

options.text: It drops to roughly 500 MB, since that is what is still live
options.why: That is VACUUM FULL's behaviour, not VACUUM's, and the distinction matters precisely when a disk is filling up. Plain VACUUM never rewrites the file.

options.text: It grows, because VACUUM writes bookkeeping about what it freed
options.why: VACUUM does write (it touches the visibility map and the free space map) but those are separate small forks, not growth of the table's own file.

quiz.prompt: In PostgreSQL an index entry points at a physical `(page, slot)` address. Given only that, why can updating one *unindexed* column of a row cause writes to five different indexes?

options.text: It cannot: Postgres skips indexes whose columns did not change
options.why: There is an optimisation in this direction, HOT (heap-only tuple) updates, but it only applies when the new version fits on the *same page*. Once the row has to move to another page, every index must be updated.

options.text: Each index stores a copy of the whole row, so all copies must be kept in sync
options.why: An index stores its own key columns plus a pointer, not the whole row. If it stored the whole row, updating an indexed column would be the expensive case, but here the expensive case is updating an *unindexed* one.

options.text: Postgres rebuilds all indexes on a table whenever any row in it changes
options.why: Nothing so drastic: the work is per-row, not per-table. A single-row update adds one entry per index, which is bad enough at scale but is not a rebuild.

options.text: The update writes the row at a new physical address, so every index that points at the old address has to be given the new one
options.why: The indexes are not stale because of what the column meant: they are stale because of where the row *is*. This write amplification was Uber's headline reason for migrating off Postgres in 2016. InnoDB dodges it by having secondary indexes point at the primary key rather than a location, paying an extra lookup on every index read instead.

quiz.prompt: What are the hidden `xmin` and `xmax` columns on a PostgreSQL row, and how do they let one transaction read a table while another rewrites it?

options.text: A read lock and a write lock held on the row while a transaction touches it
options.why: Backwards: these fields exist so that locks are *not* needed for reading. Postgres's readers-never-block-writers property comes precisely from resolving visibility by comparing ids rather than by taking a lock.

options.text: The transaction that created this row version and the one that deleted it, so each transaction can filter to the versions that were live when it started
options.why: Visibility is a comparison, not a lock. Your transaction has a snapshot; a row version is visible if its xmin committed before that snapshot and its xmax did not. Since every writer creates new versions rather than editing old ones, the versions your snapshot needs are still sitting there.

options.text: Timestamps recording when the row was inserted and last modified
options.why: Tempting, and they are used for ordering, but they are transaction ids, not times. That distinction is why they can run out: they are 32-bit counters, and the ceiling of about two billion is what makes wraparound a real operational hazard.

options.text: The minimum and maximum values of the row's indexed columns
options.why: They have nothing to do with your data. The x stands for transaction (xact); both hold transaction ids, and they are the same on a row whose columns are entirely unrelated.

hooks.remember: PostgreSQL reads and writes in 8 kB pages, never single rows.
hooks.hook: The table is a warehouse that only lends out **whole boxes**, 8 kB each. Want one row? You carry out the entire box it sits in. A `Seq Scan` is a forklift hauling every box in the building to find one sock, which is why "rows read" matters less than "pages touched".

hooks.remember: `ctid` is a physical address, `(page, slot)`, and an UPDATE moves the row to a new one.
hooks.hook: Every row is a guest at Hotel Postgres, and `ctid` is the room number: floor and door, `(page, slot)`. An `UPDATE` never redecorates. The guest checks into a **new room** with the change, and the old room keeps a ghost until housekeeping comes. So a `ctid` is where somebody is sleeping tonight, never who they are.

hooks.remember: `xmin` is the transaction that created a row version, `xmax` the one that ended it.
hooks.hook: Each row version carries two certificates: a **birth** certificate (`xmin`, the transaction that wrote it) and, once replaced or deleted, a **death** certificate (`xmax`). A reader never asks a writer for permission. It reads the dates against its own snapshot: born before I looked, not dead yet? Visible. That is how readers and writers avoid waiting for each other.

hooks.remember: Plain VACUUM makes dead space reusable but does not shrink the file; VACUUM FULL rewrites it under a lock.
hooks.hook: `VACUUM` is a janitor: it sweeps the ghost rooms and hangs **"vacant"** signs on the doors for this table's next guests. The building stays 4 GB. To shrink it you need `VACUUM FULL`, which builds a whole new hotel next door, moves everyone in, and keeps the front door **locked** the entire time.

task.markdown:
Get a PostgreSQL server in front of you and make it show you its own pages. Do not take
any of the numbers above on trust; produce them yourself.

If you have no Postgres to hand, `docker run --rm -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=x -p 5432:5432
postgres:16` and `psql -h localhost -U postgres` is a 30-second setup.

1. Confirm `block_size`, then create a table and check `pg_relation_size` before and
   after inserting a couple of thousand rows. Record where the page count jumps.
2. Select `ctid` alongside your own columns and work out how many rows are landing per
   page.
3. Update one row. Select its `ctid` again. Explain the number you get.
4. Update *every* row three times, then compare `pg_relation_size` and `count(*)`.
5. Run `VACUUM`, measure again, then `VACUUM FULL`, and measure again. Only one of them
   changes the file size. Record both numbers.

Write every number you saw into the file as a comment beside the query that produced it.
Those comments are your record of what the engine actually did.
checklist: `block_size` confirmed and the table's page count measured before and after inserts
`ctid` selected, and rows-per-page worked out from it
a single row observed changing its `ctid` after an `UPDATE`
the file measured growing while `count(*)` stayed the same
`VACUUM` and `VACUUM FULL` both measured, and you can say why only one shrank it

days.title: An index is a sorted copy
days.teaser: Same index, same query, one word different, and the planner refuses it
days.teachBack: An index is a second sorted tree, not an annotation on the table. Use that to explain both why `WHERE lower(email) = ?` cannot use an index on `email`, and why a planner that has a perfectly usable index will sometimes choose to ignore it and be right to.
days.theoryMarkdown:
Day 1 showed that a table is a heap of pages, and that finding a row without help means
reading all of them. This lesson covers what an index actually is, and the four separate reasons a perfectly good
one gets ignored.

### It is a second table you don't get to see

An index is **another B-tree**, containing the indexed columns plus a pointer back to the
row's physical location, kept sorted.

That one sentence explains most of what indexes do:

- Lookups get fast, because the tree is sorted: finding a value is a descent through
  three or four pages instead of a walk through all of them.
- Writes get slower, because every `INSERT` now writes two trees, and (as day 1's
  `ctid` section showed) an `UPDATE` that moves a row writes *every* index on the table.
- The database gets bigger, sometimes much bigger, because the index is a real copy of
  real data.
- `ORDER BY` on the indexed column can become free: the sorted order already exists on
  disk, so there is nothing to sort.

Here is the third point on a 50,000-row table with two indexes:

```
  relname  | pg_size_pretty
-----------+----------------
 idx_lower | 1544 kB
 idx_name  | 1544 kB
 s         | 4552 kB
```

Two indexes on one column each, and they are already two thirds of the size of the table
holding three columns. This is why index bloat is a real budget line, and why
`pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0` (an index nobody has ever used) is the first thing a
Postgres consultant greps for.

### Ask the planner, never guess

Every engine will tell you its plan. In Postgres:

```sql order
CREATE TABLE s(id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, name text, note text);
INSERT INTO s(name, note) SELECT 'name' || g, repeat('x', 40) FROM generate_series(1, 50000) g;
ANALYZE s;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM s WHERE name = 'name7';
```

```
                     QUERY PLAN
-----------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on s  (cost=0.00..1194.00 rows=1 width=58)
   Filter: (name = 'name7'::text)
```

`Seq Scan`: every page, to find one row. Now build the index:

```sql order
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON s(name);
ANALYZE s;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM s WHERE name = 'name7';
```

```
 Index Scan using idx_name on s  (cost=0.29..8.31 rows=1 width=58)
   Index Cond: (name = 'name7'::text)
```

Cost 1194 to cost 8.31. Note the `ANALYZE` in there. It is the *other* `ANALYZE`, separate
from `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and it updates the planner's statistics. Postgres picks plans by
estimating row counts from a sample of your data, so stale statistics are behind a lot of
"it was fast yesterday" incidents, and they are the first thing to check after a bulk load.

Two numbers, both estimates: `cost` is in arbitrary units where 1.0 is roughly one
sequential page read, and `rows` is how many the planner *thinks* will come back.
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and prints what really happened next to the guess. When a
plan looks mysterious, the gap between the estimated and the actual row count usually
explains it.

### Reason one: you asked about a different value

**An index on a column can only answer questions about that column's value.** Wrap the
column in a function and you are asking about a different value, which the sorted copy is
not sorted by.

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM s WHERE lower(name) = 'name7';
```

```
 Seq Scan on s  (cost=0.00..1319.00 rows=250 width=58)
   Filter: (lower(name) = 'name7'::text)
```

`Seq Scan`, with `idx_name` sitting right there. Same story for `WHERE price * 1.2 > 100`,
`WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-01-01'`, and every `WHERE CAST(id AS text) = ?` written to
make a type error go away. Postgres's answer is to let you index the expression itself:

```sql order
CREATE INDEX idx_lower ON s(lower(name));
ANALYZE s;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM s WHERE lower(name) = 'name7';
```

```
 Index Scan using idx_lower on s  (cost=0.29..8.31 rows=1 width=58)
   Index Cond: (lower(name) = 'name7'::text)
```

MySQL only got expression indexes in 8.0.13, in 2018. The case-insensitive email index
above is one of the most common uses of them.

### Reason two: the index would be slower

One table, one index and one query shape. Only the *value* changes:

```
=== WHERE status = 'rare'      (2,000 of 200,000 rows)
 Index Only Scan using idx_status on t2 (actual time=0.033..1.644 rows=2000 loops=1)
 Execution Time: 1.788 ms

=== WHERE status = 'common'    (198,000 of 200,000 rows)
 Parallel Seq Scan on t2 (actual time=0.016..13.148 rows=99000 loops=2)
 Execution Time: 24.699 ms
```

The planner used the index for `'rare'` and *refused* it for `'common'`, and it was right
both times. An index scan costs one descent per matching row, plus a jump to the heap for
each; once you are fetching most of the table, reading it straight through in physical
order is cheaper than 198,000 random jumps. This is why "add an index" does nothing for
your `WHERE deleted = false` filter when 99% of rows are not deleted, and why a partial
index (`CREATE INDEX ... WHERE deleted = true`) is often the answer.

### Reason three: the query needed a column the index doesn't carry

If the index contains every column the query needs, the engine can answer from the index
alone and never touch the heap:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM s WHERE name = 'name7';
```

```
 Index Only Scan using idx_name on s  (cost=0.29..8.31 rows=1 width=9)
```

Look for `Index Only Scan` in the plan: it means the second lookup, index to row, did not
happen. Change that `SELECT name` to `SELECT *` and it drops back to a plain
`Index Scan`, because `note` only exists in the heap. This is why adding one more column
to an existing index sometimes beats adding a whole new index, and Postgres has dedicated
syntax for exactly that: `CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (note)` carries the extra column in the
index's leaf pages without making it part of the sort key.

> [!NOTE]
> Index-only scans in Postgres are only *mostly* index-only. The index has no visibility
> information, so the engine still has to know whether each row is visible to your
> transaction. It consults the **visibility map**, one bit per page saying "everything on
> this page is visible to everyone". Pages the map hasn't marked force a heap fetch
> anyway. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` prints `Heap Fetches:`, and a high number there on a
> supposedly index-only scan almost always means the table needs vacuuming. Two lessons
> in and vacuum is already the answer to a second unrelated question.

### Worth knowing: `C.UTF-8` is not `C`, and the difference is a sequential scan

A prefix search looks like it should be a range scan, since everything starting with
`name7` is contiguous in a sorted list. It isn't:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM s WHERE name LIKE 'name7%';
```

```
 Seq Scan on s  (cost=0.00..1194.00 rows=1010 width=58)
   Filter: (name ~~ 'name7%'::text)
```

The reason is **collation**. An index is sorted according to some collation, and a
locale-aware one (`en_US.UTF-8`, and yes `C.UTF-8`) can sort in ways where the strings
matching a prefix are not one contiguous run, so `LIKE 'x%'` cannot be turned into a
range. Only the `C` collation, which compares byte by byte, guarantees it can.

The trap is that `C.UTF-8` *looks* like `C` and is not. Prove it by declaring an index
with the real thing:

```sql order
CREATE INDEX idx_c ON s(name COLLATE "C");
ANALYZE s;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM s WHERE name LIKE 'name7%';
```

```
 Bitmap Heap Scan on s  (cost=26.44..624.27 rows=1010 width=58)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_c  (cost=0.00..26.19 rows=990 width=0)
         Index Cond: ((name >= 'name7'::text) AND (name < 'name8'::text))
```

Look at what the planner did with your `LIKE`: it rewrote it into `name >= 'name7' AND
name < 'name8'`, a range, exactly as the intuition said it should. The equivalent without
touching collation is a `text_pattern_ops` index, which sorts by byte regardless of the
database's locale.

Two more things to carry out of this. First, the plan is a **Bitmap Heap Scan**, Postgres's
middle gear for when a few thousand rows match: it collects all their locations first,
sorts them into physical order, then sweeps the heap once. Second, a database created with
a locale-aware collation will *silently* not use your index for prefix searches, and people
usually find out in production, the week after it worked on a laptop where the default
was different.

CREATE TABLE s(id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, name text, note text);
INSERT INTO s(name, note) SELECT 'name' || g, repeat('x', 40) FROM generate_series(1, 2000) g;

CREATE TABLE users (
  id       int PRIMARY KEY,
  email    text NOT NULL,
  country  text NOT NULL,
  deleted  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);
INSERT INTO users VALUES
  (1, 'ana@mail.io', 'DE', false),
  (2, 'bo@mail.io',  'FR', false),
  (3, 'cy@mail.io',  'US', false),
  (4, 'dee@mail.io', 'UZ', false),
  (5, 'eli@mail.io', 'DE', true),
  (6, 'fay@mail.io', 'FR', false),
  (7, 'deena@mail.io', 'UZ', false);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     int NOT NULL REFERENCES users,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  amount      numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  code        text NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO orders
SELECT g,
       g % 6 + 1,
       (ARRAY['paid', 'paid', 'pending', 'cancelled', 'paid'])[g % 5 + 1],
       (g * 37 % 200) + 0.50,
       (ARRAY['AB', 'CBX', 'BX'])[g % 3 + 1] || lpad(g::text, 4, '0'),
       -- two orders per timestamp: ties are what make paging and ranges honest
       timestamptz '2026-03-01 08:00+00' + ((g + 1) / 2) * interval '14 hours'
FROM generate_series(1, 24) g;
CREATE INDEX orders_status_idx ON orders (status);

challenges.prompt: Every page of the app loads a user's orders with `WHERE user_id = $1`, and PostgreSQL does not index a foreign key for you. Create the index on `orders` that serves that lookup.
challenges.solution: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id);
challenges.hint: A foreign key constrains the column; it does not make it searchable.
challenges.verify:
SELECT regexp_replace(indexdef, 'INDEX \S+ ON ', 'INDEX ON ') AS definition
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND indexname NOT IN ('orders_pkey', 'orders_status_idx')
ORDER BY 1;

challenges.prompt: Two accounts must never share an email. Enforce it on `users.email` with an index.
challenges.solution: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email);
challenges.hint: An index can refuse duplicates as well as find things.

challenges.prompt: `Ana@Mail.io` and `ana@mail.io` are the same mailbox. Make it impossible for two users to have emails that differ only in letter case.
challenges.solution: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (lower(email));
challenges.hint: The uniqueness has to be about a value computed from the column.

challenges.prompt: The hottest query is `WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at`. Create the one two-column index that serves both the filter and the sort, so no sort step is needed.
challenges.solution: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, created_at);
challenges.hint: The column you test with `=` goes first; within one user, the rows then come out sorted by the second.
challenges.verify:
SELECT string_agg(a.attname, ', ' ORDER BY k.ord) AS key_columns
FROM pg_index i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(i.indkey::int2[]) WITH ORDINALITY AS k(attnum, ord)
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = k.attnum
WHERE i.indrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND c.relname NOT IN ('orders_pkey', 'orders_status_idx')
GROUP BY c.relname;

challenges.prompt: A report runs `ORDER BY user_id, created_at DESC`. A plain `(user_id, created_at)` index can't produce that order, so Postgres sorts. Create a two-column index that can produce it directly.
challenges.solution: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
challenges.hint: Each column of an index has its own direction. Read it forwards or backwards: what order do you need?
challenges.verify:
SELECT string_agg(a.attname, ', ' ORDER BY k.ord) AS key_columns,
       (i.indoption[0] & 1) <> (i.indoption[1] & 1) AS directions_differ
FROM pg_index i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(i.indkey::int2[]) WITH ORDINALITY AS k(attnum, ord)
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = k.attnum
WHERE i.indrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND c.relname NOT IN ('orders_pkey', 'orders_status_idx')
GROUP BY c.relname, i.indoption;

challenges.prompt: Only *pending* orders are ever looked up by `created_at`, and they are a small slice of the table. Create an index on `created_at` that contains pending orders and nothing else.

SELECT regexp_replace(indexdef, 'INDEX \S+ ON ', 'INDEX ON ') AS definition
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND indexname NOT IN ('orders_pkey', 'orders_status_idx')

challenges.prompt: A user may have any number of paid orders but at most **one** order with status `'cart'`. Enforce that with a single index.
challenges.solution: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON orders (user_id) WHERE status = 'cart';
challenges.hint: Unique, but only among some of the rows.
challenges.verify:
SELECT regexp_replace(indexdef, 'INDEX \S+ ON ', 'INDEX ON ') AS definition
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND indexname NOT IN ('orders_pkey', 'orders_status_idx')
ORDER BY 1;

challenges.prompt: `SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1` should be answered from the index alone, with no trip to the table. Create one index keyed on `user_id` that also carries `amount`, without making `amount` part of the sort key.
challenges.solution: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id) INCLUDE (amount);
challenges.hint: There is a clause for columns that ride along in the leaf pages.

SELECT regexp_replace(indexdef, 'INDEX \S+ ON ', 'INDEX ON ') AS definition
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND indexname NOT IN ('orders_pkey', 'orders_status_idx')
ORDER BY 1;

challenges.prompt: `WHERE code LIKE 'AB%'` has to use an index whatever the database's collation is, and you may not change the column's collation. Create that index on `code`.
challenges.solution: CREATE INDEX ON orders (code text_pattern_ops);
challenges.hint: An index column can name an operator class that compares byte by byte.

SELECT regexp_replace(indexdef, 'INDEX \S+ ON ', 'INDEX ON ') AS definition
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND indexname NOT IN ('orders_pkey', 'orders_status_idx')

drill.tag: when the planner skips an index
drill.code:
-- 200,000 rows; 1% have deleted = true. There is an index on (deleted).
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM t WHERE deleted = false;
drill.prompt: Which plan comes back on PostgreSQL 16?

options.text: `Index Scan using t_deleted`: there is an index on exactly that column
options.why: An index existing is not a reason to use it. For 198,000 matching rows, 198,000 random heap fetches lose to one sequential pass.

options.text: `Bitmap Heap Scan`: a middle gear for many rows
options.why: A bitmap scan is for a few thousand rows. At 99% of the table there is nothing to gain from sorting the locations first: every page is needed anyway.

options.text: `Seq Scan on t` with `Filter: (NOT deleted)`
options.why: 99% of the table matches. Reading it straight through is far cheaper than one index lookup and one random heap jump per row, so the planner ignores the index: correctly. The same index *is* used for `deleted = true`, the rare value.

drill.code: CREATE INDEX ON t (country, created_at);
drill.prompt: Which condition lets PostgreSQL 16 jump straight to the matching entries of this index?

options.text: `WHERE country = 'DE' AND created_at > '2026-04-01'`
options.why: The index is sorted by country first, then by created_at within each country. An equality on the first column and a range on the second is one contiguous run of entries: descend once, read until the range ends.

options.text: `WHERE created_at > '2026-04-01'`
options.why: Matching created_at values are scattered across every country's section, so there is no single place to start. PostgreSQL 16 can still walk the *whole* index checking each entry, but it can't seek. (PostgreSQL 18 added B-tree *skip scan*, which hops from one country to the next: worth it when the leading column has few distinct values.)

options.text: `WHERE country > 'T' AND created_at = '2026-03-01'`
options.why: A range on the first column means the second column is no longer sorted across the run, so only the `country` part narrows the search; `created_at` is checked entry by entry inside it.

drill.prompt: The first plan says `Index Only Scan using t_name`. What does the second say?

options.text: `Index Scan using t_name`: it has to visit the table for the other columns
options.why: `SELECT *` needs columns that live only in the heap, so each match costs a second lookup, from index entry to row. Selecting only what the index holds skips it.

options.text: `Index Only Scan using t_name`: the WHERE clause is the same
options.why: The WHERE clause decides how rows are found; the SELECT list decides whether the table has to be visited to finish them. `*` includes columns the index lacks.

options.text: `Seq Scan on t`: `SELECT *` is too wide for an index
options.why: One matching row is cheap to fetch from the heap. The index is still used to find it; only the extra hop to the table is added.

drill.code:
CREATE INDEX ON t (name);
SELECT * FROM t WHERE name LIKE '%77';
drill.prompt: Can a B-tree index on `name` help this query?

options.text: Yes: LIKE always uses an index when one exists on the column
options.why: Only a pattern with a fixed prefix can be rewritten into a range, and only under the C collation or a pattern-ops index.

options.text: Yes, if the index uses `text_pattern_ops`
options.why: `text_pattern_ops` makes *prefix* matches indexable under any collation. A leading wildcard is still a scan of everything.

options.text: No: a sorted list can't find values by how they end; a trigram (`pg_trgm`) GIN index can
options.why: A B-tree is sorted from the first character. Everything starting with "name7" is one run; everything ending in "77" is scattered across the whole list. On PG16 the plan is `Seq Scan` with `Filter: (name ~~ '%77'::text)`.

drill.code:
CREATE INDEX t_created ON t (created_at);   -- ascending
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
drill.prompt: What does PostgreSQL 16 do about the descending order?

options.text: `Limit` over `Sort` over `Seq Scan`: the index is ascending
options.why: Direction only matters when *columns disagree* (`a, b DESC`). One column can be read either way.

options.text: `Limit` over `Index Scan Backward using t_created`: no sort at all
options.why: A B-tree's leaf pages are linked both ways, so reading it from the far end gives descending order for free. A separate `DESC` index on a single column buys nothing.

options.text: An error: the index has to be declared DESC to be used for DESC
options.why: Index direction never causes an error; at worst it means a sort step. Here it doesn't even cost that.

drill.code:
CREATE INDEX ON t (user_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY user_id, created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
drill.prompt: What appears above the index scan in the plan?

options.text: A full `Sort` over a `Seq Scan`
options.why: That was the only option before PostgreSQL 13. Now the planner can use the part of the order the index already provides.

options.text: Nothing: `Index Scan Backward` handles the DESC
options.why: Backwards gives `user_id DESC, created_at DESC`. You asked for user_id ascending *and* created_at descending; no single direction of this index produces that.

options.text: `Incremental Sort` with `Presorted Key: user_id`
options.why: The index already delivers rows grouped by user_id; only within each user does the order need flipping. Incremental sort (PostgreSQL 13+) sorts one small group at a time. An index `(user_id, created_at DESC)` would remove even that.

drill.prompt: Why does the index go unused?

options.text: The planner expects too many matching rows for an index to pay off
options.why: The same lookup written as `code = 'BX000003'` uses the index for one row. Nothing about the data changed, only what the condition is about.

options.text: The condition is about `lower(code)`, a value the index does not hold and is not sorted by
options.why: The index is a sorted copy of `code`. To use it the planner needs a condition on `code` itself. `WHERE code = 'BX000003'` plans `Index Scan using t_code` on PostgreSQL 16; if case really varies, index the expression: `CREATE INDEX ON t (lower(code))`.

options.text: Functions are not allowed on an indexed column, so PostgreSQL ignores the index
options.why: Functions are allowed anywhere; the query runs and is correct. It is just that only an index built on that same expression can answer it.

drill.code:
CREATE INDEX t_pending ON t (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM t WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at > '2026-04-01';
drill.prompt: Can `t_pending` be used here?

options.text: Yes, then it filters for paid
options.why: The paid rows aren't in it at all. Using it would silently return nothing, which is exactly the mistake the implication rule prevents.

options.text: Yes: partial indexes are used for any query on their key column
options.why: The predicate is part of the index's meaning. Same query with `status = 'pending'`: `Index Scan using t_pending`.

options.text: No: it holds only pending rows, so it can't answer a question about paid ones
options.why: The planner may use a partial index only when the query's WHERE *implies* the index's WHERE. `status = 'paid'` does not imply `status = 'pending'`.

drill.prompt: What happens?

options.text: Both inserts succeed and the count is 2
options.why: A unique index compares values, and NULL is not equal to NULL, so two NULLs are not duplicates. Since PostgreSQL 15 you can say `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` when you want at most one.

options.text: The first insert fails: a unique column can't be NULL
options.why: UNIQUE and NOT NULL are separate constraints. A PRIMARY KEY is both; a unique index is only the first.

options.text: The second insert fails with a duplicate key error
options.why: That is what `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG15+) does. The default treats every NULL as distinct.

drill.prompt: What does the count say?

options.text: 2: EXPLAIN only shows a plan
options.why: Plain `EXPLAIN` only plans. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes, which is the only way it can report actual rows and times.

options.text: An error: EXPLAIN only accepts SELECT
options.why: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE can all be explained, and analysed, with their effects.

options.text: 0: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` really runs the statement
options.why: ANALYZE means "execute it and measure". The plan printed `Seq Scan on u (actual rows=2 …)` and the rows are gone. Wrap it in `BEGIN; … ROLLBACK;` whenever you analyse a write.

drill.tag: when the planner skips an index
drill.prompt: Why an index scan for nearly the whole table, and what fixes it?

options.text: Postgres always prefers an index when one exists; drop it
options.why: Run `ANALYZE b` and the very same query plans a sequential scan. The choice is cost-based, and the cost was computed from stale numbers.

options.text: The index is corrupted; `REINDEX` fixes it
options.why: The index is fine and complete. The *estimate* is wrong, and estimates come from statistics, not from the index.

options.text: The statistics still describe the 10-row table; `ANALYZE b` and the plan becomes `Seq Scan`
options.why: The planner never reads your data to plan: it reads the sample `ANALYZE` took, which says every k is 1, so `k > 5` "matches nothing". Autovacuum would analyze eventually; after a bulk load, do it yourself.

drill.prompt: How many B-trees does that one INSERT write to, besides the table itself?

options.text: One, only the primary key is maintained on insert; the others are updated lazily
options.why: B-tree indexes in PostgreSQL are maintained synchronously, in the same transaction. (GIN has a "pending list" that defers work; B-tree has no such thing.)

options.text: Three: the primary key's index and both others
options.why: Every index is a separate sorted copy, and each must gain an entry for the new row. This is the cost side of every index: reads get cheaper, every write gets a little dearer, forever.

options.text: None: indexes are rebuilt by VACUUM
options.why: VACUUM removes dead entries; it never adds new ones. A row is findable through an index the moment its transaction commits.

quiz.prompt: You add an index to speed up a slow report. Name two distinct costs you have just taken on.

options.text: Every write to the table now maintains a second tree, and the index occupies real disk space of its own
options.why: Those are the two standing costs, and neither is small. Two single-column indexes on a three-column 50,000-row table came to 1544 kB each against a 4552 kB table: two thirds of the table's size, for two columns. And in PostgreSQL the write cost is worse than it first looks: because index entries hold a physical row location, an UPDATE that moves a row must touch every index on the table, not just the ones on columns you changed.

options.text: Queries that do not use the index have to skip past it while scanning
options.why: An index is a separate file. A sequential scan of the table never reads it and never steps over it.

options.text: The table must be locked whenever the index is used
options.why: Reading through an index takes no special lock. There is a locking cost to *building* one, which is why CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY exists, but that is a one-off, not a cost of having the index.

options.text: Reads of other columns get slower, because the row is now split in two
options.why: The row is not split. The index is an additional copy of the indexed columns; the heap still holds every column exactly as before, and reads that ignore the index are unaffected.

quiz.prompt: A query filters on an indexed column and the plan still shows `Seq Scan`, even though the index exists and the column is right. Give two different reasons that can happen.

options.text: The column is nullable, and PostgreSQL cannot index columns that contain NULLs
options.why: PostgreSQL B-trees do index NULLs, and `WHERE col IS NULL` can use an index. (This is a real difference between engines (Oracle's B-trees famously omit all-NULL keys) but it is not why Postgres would choose a Seq Scan.)

options.text: The filter wraps the column in a function or a cast, or the value matches so many rows that scanning is genuinely cheaper
options.why: Two entirely different failures that produce the identical symptom. The first is a correctness limit: an index on `name` is sorted by `name`, so it can say nothing about `lower(name)`. The second is the planner being right: fetching 198,000 of 200,000 rows through an index means 198,000 random heap jumps, and reading the table straight through beat it by more than 10x in the lesson's measurement.

options.text: The index has not finished building, or the table has too few rows for an index to exist
options.why: An unfinished CREATE INDEX is simply not visible to the planner yet, so this is not really a case of an index being ignored. And no row-count threshold governs whether an index can exist: small tables just rarely benefit.

options.text: The statistics are stale, which makes the index physically unusable
options.why: Stale statistics are a genuine and very common cause of a bad plan, but they mislead the planner's *estimate*, they do not make an index unusable. Run ANALYZE and the same index may suddenly be chosen for the same query.

quiz.prompt: What does `Index Only Scan` mean in a PostgreSQL plan, what work does it save, and what can still force it to touch the heap anyway?

options.text: The index carried every column the query needed, so the heap lookup was skipped: except for pages the visibility map has not marked all-visible
options.why: The saving is the second lookup: index entry to row. The catch is that an index holds no visibility information, so Postgres must still establish that each row is visible to your transaction. It uses the visibility map, one bit per page, and any page not marked forces a heap fetch after all. EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints `Heap Fetches:`, and a large number there usually means the table wants vacuuming.

options.text: Only one index was used, rather than combining several
options.why: Combining indexes is a real Postgres capability, but it shows up as a BitmapAnd or BitmapOr over Bitmap Index Scans. "Index Only" refers to not visiting the heap.

options.text: The query was answered from the index because the table itself was locked by another transaction
options.why: Plan choice has nothing to do with locks held elsewhere. The planner picks this shape purely because the index happens to contain every column required.

options.text: The whole index was loaded into memory, so no disk reads were needed
options.why: "Only" describes which structures were consulted, not where they live. An Index Only Scan still reads index pages from disk if they are not cached.

quiz.prompt: Your table has an index on `email`. Which of `WHERE email = ?`, `WHERE lower(email) = ?` and `WHERE email LIKE 'a%'` can use it, and what decides the last one?

options.text: Equality and `LIKE 'a%'`; `lower(email)` works too once the statistics are refreshed
options.why: ANALYZE cannot help here. There is no entry anywhere in an index on `email` that records what `lower(email)` is, so no amount of better estimation makes that index answer the question. You need a second index, on the expression.

options.text: Only the equality one; B-trees answer equality and nothing else
options.why: B-trees are excellent at ranges: that is what being sorted buys you. `>`, `<`, `BETWEEN` and `ORDER BY` all use them, and a prefix `LIKE` is a range in disguise when the collation permits.

options.text: All three, since all three mention only the indexed column
options.why: Mentioning the column is not the test. The test is whether the query's condition can be expressed as a range over the *order the index is sorted in*, which `lower(email)` cannot be, at any collation.

options.text: Equality yes; `lower(email)` no, without an index on the expression; `LIKE 'a%'` only if the index's collation is `C` or it uses `text_pattern_ops`
options.why: The first two follow from the index being sorted by `email` and nothing else. The third is the subtle one: turning `LIKE 'a%'` into the range `>= 'a' AND < 'b'` is only valid if the sort order is bytewise. A locale-aware collation may interleave strings so that the prefix matches are not contiguous, and `C.UTF-8` counts as locale-aware, despite the name.

quiz.prompt: `EXPLAIN` says a query will return 3 rows; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows it actually returned 40,000. What is most likely wrong, and what does the planner do with a bad estimate?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; `EXPLAIN` reports rows examined and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` reports rows returned
options.why: Both report the same quantity: rows emitted by that node. One is the planner's estimate and the other is the measured truth, which is exactly why comparing them is useful.

options.text: The query changed between the two runs, so the numbers are not comparable
options.why: EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans and executes the same statement, so the estimate and the actual come from one run. They are directly comparable by design.

options.text: The planner notices the discrepancy mid-execution and re-plans with the real number
options.why: PostgreSQL does not re-plan mid-execution; the plan is fixed before the first row is produced, and a bad estimate is lived with to the end. Adaptive re-planning of this kind exists in some other systems, but assuming it here is how people conclude a plan "should have fixed itself".

options.text: The statistics are stale or unrepresentative, and since the estimate is what chooses the plan, a wrong one picks a plan suited to a query that does not exist
options.why: This gap is where nearly every planner mystery is solved, which is why you reach for EXPLAIN ANALYZE rather than EXPLAIN. Believing three rows, the planner happily picks an index scan or a nested loop; at 40,000 rows those become 40,000 random jumps or 40,000 inner scans. ANALYZE after a bulk load is the first thing to try, and correlated columns, where the planner assumes independence and is wrong, are the next suspect.

hooks.remember: An index on `email` cannot serve `WHERE lower(email) = …`; keep the column bare, or index the expression.
hooks.hook: The index is a phone book sorted by `email` **exactly as stored**. Wrap the column in a glove (`lower(email)`) and you are asking for a book sorted by something else, which does not exist, so Postgres reads every page. Two cures: put the function on the *other* side (`email = lower($1)`), or print the book you want: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))`.

hooks.remember: A composite index on `(a, b)` helps queries on `a`, or `a` and `b`, but not on `b` alone.
hooks.hook: An index on `(last_name, first_name)` is the old phone book. "Smith"? Instant. "Smith, Anna"? Instant. "Everyone called Anna"? The Annas are scattered across every surname, so the book is just a heavy brick. **Leftmost column first**, always.

hooks.remember: `LIKE 'abc%'` can use a B-tree index; `LIKE '%abc'` cannot.
hooks.hook: A sorted index is a **dictionary**: words that *start* with "abc" sit together on one page. Words that *end* in "abc" are a **crossword** clue, and the only way to solve it is to read the whole dictionary. A leading `%` throws the sort away. (For endings, a trigram index, `pg_trgm`, is the tool.)

hooks.remember: An Index Only Scan still visits the table for pages the visibility map has not marked all-visible (`Heap Fetches`).
hooks.hook: The index knows values but not who is **alive**: life and death live in the heap's `xmin`/`xmax`. The visibility map is a list of pages where "everyone here is alive". For any page not on the list, Postgres must walk over and **knock on the heap's door**. Every knock is a `Heap Fetch`. VACUUM is what adds pages to the list.

hooks.remember: The planner chooses from estimates (statistics sampled by ANALYZE), and fetching many rows through an index can cost more than a Seq Scan.
hooks.hook: The planner never reads your data. It reads the **census** `ANALYZE` last took, and bets. After a bulk load the census is stale, and it bets on a town of 3 people that now holds 40,000. And even with a fresh census: fetching a big share of the table through an index is one courier trip **per row**. Past a few percent, driving the truck down every aisle (`Seq Scan`) is cheaper.
tags: when the planner skips an index

task.markdown:
Prove each of these to yourself rather than taking the lesson's word for it. Use enough
rows that the planner has a real decision to make: 50,000 is plenty, and
`generate_series` will produce them in one statement.

1. `EXPLAIN` an equality filter with no index. Record the plan and its cost.
2. Add the index, `ANALYZE`, run it again, and record how both changed.
3. Wrap the column in `lower()` and watch it fall back to a sequential scan.
4. Add an expression index and watch it recover.
5. Get one query to report `Index Only Scan`, then change it so the same index gives you

6. Build a column where one value is rare and one is common, index it, and find the query

   compare the execution times. The refusal should be the faster one.

days.title: NULL is not a value
days.teaser: The query that returned zero rows for two years and never logged an error
days.teachBack: Walk through why `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` returns nothing for every possible `x`. Expand the expression, say what each term evaluates to, and explain why `WHERE` then drops the row, including why it drops it silently rather than erroring.
days.theoryMarkdown:
Two lessons about where bytes live. This one is about a single value that isn't one, and
the class of bug it produces: queries that are syntactically perfect, throw no error, log
nothing, and return the wrong answer for years.

### NULL means unknown

`NULL` means *unknown*. It is neither zero nor an empty string, and it is not a default
either. Once you take that literally, everything else follows, including the parts that
look broken.

If a value is unknown, then any comparison with it is also unknown:

```sql
SELECT NULL = NULL AS "null = null", NULL <> NULL AS "null <> null", NULL IS NULL AS "is null";
```

```
 null = null | null <> null | is null
-------------+--------------+---------
             |              | t
```

The first two came back blank, which is how psql prints NULL. `NULL = NULL` is unknown,
because two unknown quantities may or may not be equal and SQL declines to guess. This is why `IS NULL` exists as separate syntax: it is the only
operator that asks about the unknown-ness itself rather than about the value.

So SQL conditions have three possible results: true, false and unknown. This is called
**three-valued logic**, and one rule turns it into production bugs:

> `WHERE` keeps a row only when the condition is **true**. Unknown is discarded, exactly
> like false.

Nothing warns you when that happens.

### The query that returns nothing, forever

Three users, and one of the two orders has a NULL `user_id` (a returns row, a deleted
account, a legacy import, whatever your schema permits):

```sql
CREATE TABLE users(id int, name text);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ana'), (2, 'bo'), (3, 'cy');
```

```sql order
CREATE TABLE orders(id int, user_id int);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10, 1), (11, NULL);
SELECT name FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);
```

```
 name
------
(0 rows)
```

Two users have never ordered anything. The query says nobody has. It is a perfectly
reasonable-looking way to ask the question, it returns a perfectly reasonable-looking
empty result, and it is wrong.

Expand it for user 2. `2 NOT IN (1, NULL)` means `2 <> 1 AND 2 <> NULL`:

```
 2=1 | 2=NULL | not in
-----+--------+--------
 f   |        |
```

`2 <> 1` is true. `2 <> NULL` is **unknown**. And `true AND unknown` is unknown, so
`WHERE` drops the row. Now notice that nothing about this depended on the
number 2. Whatever value you test, the second term stays unknown, so the whole `NOT IN`
is at best unknown and the row is always dropped. A single NULL anywhere in the list
makes `NOT IN` return nothing for every possible input.

`IN` is not symmetric with it: `2 IN (1, NULL)` is also unknown and also drops the row,
but at least it can return true when there *is* a match, so the bug hides only the misses.
`NOT IN` hides everything.

The fix is `NOT EXISTS`, which is written in terms of rows rather than values and so has
nothing to be unknown about:

```sql
SELECT name FROM users WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = users.id);
```

```
 name
------
 bo
 cy
```

Postgres will also usually plan `NOT EXISTS` better (as an anti-join rather than as a
filter), so here the correct version is generally the faster one too.

### It is contagious

Unknown propagates through arithmetic and string operations as well as comparisons:

```sql
SELECT 'a' || NULL AS concat, 1 + NULL AS arith, coalesce('a' || NULL, 'fallback') AS fixed;
```

```
 concat | arith |  fixed
--------+-------+----------
        |       | fallback
```

`'a' || NULL` is NULL, not `'a'`. If one part of the greeting you are building is
unknown, the greeting is unknown. This is a common cause of templates that render an empty
string where a name should be, and `coalesce(x, fallback)`, which returns its first
non-NULL argument, is the standard defence.

Aggregates go the other way and **skip NULLs entirely**, which causes a second kind of
quiet error:

```sql order
CREATE TABLE n(v int);
INSERT INTO n VALUES (1), (2), (NULL);
SELECT count(*), count(v), sum(v), avg(v) FROM n;
```

```
 count | count | sum |       avg
-------+-------+-----+--------------------
     3 |     2 |   3 | 1.5000000000000000
```

`count(*)` counts rows: 3. `count(v)` counts non-NULL values: 2. And `avg` is 1.5, not 1,
because it divided by 2 rather than 3. If those NULLs represent "sensor was offline", the
average you just reported is the average of the readings you have, which is a defensible
answer. If they represent "we forgot to record a zero", it is wrong, and neither the
database nor the dashboard can tell which case you are in.

### The inconsistency experts argue about

SQL does not treat NULLs the same way everywhere. `WHERE v = NULL` matches nothing, because two unknowns are not known
to be equal. Put a second NULL into that same table and ask two more questions of it:

```sql
INSERT INTO n VALUES (NULL);
SELECT v, count(*) FROM n GROUP BY v ORDER BY v;
SELECT count(DISTINCT v) AS distinct_v, count(*) AS all_rows FROM n;
```

```
 v | count            distinct_v | all_rows
---+-------           ------------+----------
 1 |     1                     2 |        4
 2 |     1
   |     2
```

`GROUP BY` collected the two NULL rows into **one group of two**, treating them as equal
to each other in a language where `NULL = NULL` is not true. Meanwhile `count(DISTINCT v)`
ignored them entirely and reported 2 distinct values out of 4 rows. `ORDER BY` has an opinion too:
Postgres sorts NULLs as larger than every value, so they land last ascending and first
descending, and `ORDER BY x NULLS FIRST` exists because the standard left it to the
implementation.

So NULLs are unequal in `WHERE`, equal in `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT`, absent from
aggregates, and last-by-default in `ORDER BY`. Four different answers to "are two unknowns
the same thing", inside one language.

That inconsistency has kept an argument going in database theory for decades.
C. J. Date, who has spent four decades writing about the relational model and worked with
Codd himself, argues that nulls should be removed from it outright: that three-valued
logic makes queries mean things their authors cannot predict, and that missing information
belongs in additional relations rather than in a magic value. Others disagree. Claude
Rubinson's *Nulls, three-valued logic, and ambiguity
in SQL* (SIGMOD Record, 2007) argues Date misreads his own example queries, while
conceding the broader point: nulls introduce a startling amount of complexity into
apparently straightforward queries. Neither side defends the current rules as good
design, and the rules are what your queries run under.

### Worth knowing: UNIQUE lets in as many NULLs as you like, unless you say otherwise

A `UNIQUE` constraint is defined in terms of equality, and NULLs are never equal, so:

```sql order
CREATE TABLE u(v int UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO u VALUES (NULL), (NULL), (NULL);
SELECT count(*) FROM u;
```

```
 count
-------
     3
```

Three NULLs in a unique column, no error. This is the standard's behaviour, but it is not
what "unique" means to most people reading your schema, and it is one reason partial
unique indexes and `NOT NULL` on key columns are so common.

PostgreSQL 15 finally added the other option:

```sql
CREATE TABLE u2(v int UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT);
INSERT INTO u2 VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO u2 VALUES (NULL);
```

```
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "u2_v_key"
DETAIL:  Key (v)=(null) already exists.
```

`NULLS NOT DISTINCT` says: for the purpose of this constraint, treat unknowns as equal to
each other. PostgreSQL shipped it in 2022, thirty-six years after the first SQL standard.

One more tool worth carrying: `IS DISTINCT FROM` is `<>` with unknowns treated as
comparable, so `WHERE v IS DISTINCT FROM 1` returns the NULL rows as well as the 2s.
That is usually what the person writing `WHERE v <> 1` meant.

challenges.prompt: Which users have never placed an order? Return their names. `orders.user_id` can be NULL, so don't use `NOT IN`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name FROM users
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = users.id);
challenges.hint: Ask about the existence of rows, not about the equality of values.

challenges.prompt: From `n`, return in one row: how many rows there are, how many of them have a non-NULL `v`, and the average of `v`.
challenges.solution: SELECT count(*), count(v), avg(v) FROM n;
challenges.hint: One form of `count` counts rows, the other counts values.

challenges.prompt: Return every row of `n` whose `v` is not 1: **including** the row where `v` is NULL. `v <> 1` drops it.
challenges.solution: SELECT * FROM n WHERE v IS DISTINCT FROM 1;
challenges.hint: There is a comparison operator that treats unknowns as comparable.

challenges.prompt: Return each user's name and city, showing `'unknown'` where the city is NULL. Order by `id`.
challenges.solution: SELECT name, coalesce(city, 'unknown') AS city FROM users ORDER BY id;
challenges.hint: One function returns its first non-NULL argument.

quiz.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does `NULL = NULL` evaluate to, and what does `WHERE` do with a row whose condition evaluates to that?

options.text: False, and the row is discarded
options.why: The row is discarded, but the reason matters enormously. If it were false you could rely on `NOT (NULL = NULL)` being true, and it is not, it is unknown too. That is precisely how NOT IN goes wrong.

options.text: True, since both sides are identical
options.why: Identical *syntax*, not identical values. NULL is not a value that can be equal to anything, including another NULL, which is why `IS NULL` had to be invented as separate syntax.

options.text: Unknown, a third truth value, and `WHERE` discards the row, exactly as it would for false
options.why: NULL means unknown, so whether two unknowns are equal is itself unknown. SQL runs on three-valued logic, and `WHERE` keeps a row only when the condition is *true*. Because unknown and false are discarded identically and silently, a query built on unknowns returns a plausible-looking result and logs nothing.

options.text: It raises an error, which is why `IS NULL` exists
options.why: No error is raised, and that is the whole danger. An error would be a gift; you would find it in a log. Instead the expression evaluates to unknown and the row silently vanishes.

quiz.prompt: Walk through why `WHERE x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` returns no rows for every possible value of `x`.

options.text: `NOT IN` cannot be used with subqueries that return NULL, so PostgreSQL returns an empty set
options.why: Nothing special-cases NULL here and nothing is refused. The empty result is the ordinary evaluation of ordinary three-valued logic, which is exactly why it is so hard to spot.

options.text: It expands to `x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL`; the last term is always unknown, so the whole conjunction is at best unknown and never true
options.why: The important part is that this does not depend on x. Even when x is 7 and both real comparisons are true, `true AND true AND unknown` is unknown, and `WHERE` keeps only true. One NULL anywhere in the list disables the entire predicate for every input. `NOT EXISTS` is the fix, because it asks about the existence of rows rather than the equality of values.

options.text: The NULL matches every value, so every row is excluded by the NOT
options.why: A tidy story that gives the right answer for the wrong reason, and it will mislead you next time. NULL matches nothing: the comparison yields unknown, not a match. If NULL genuinely matched everything, plain `IN` would return every row, and it returns none.

options.text: The list is sorted for the lookup and NULL sorts before everything, truncating it
options.why: No sorting or truncation is involved. `IN` against a literal list is a chain of equality comparisons; the outcome comes from what those comparisons evaluate to.

quiz.prompt: A column `v` holds the values 1, 2 and NULL. What do `count(*)`, `count(v)` and `avg(v)` return, and why can that make a dashboard wrong without anything failing?

options.text: An error, since an average cannot be computed over an unknown value
options.why: No error. Aggregates over columns containing NULLs are entirely routine: the risk is a plausible number, not a failure. (`avg` over *no* non-NULL rows at all returns NULL rather than raising.)

options.text: 3, 2 and NULL: one unknown input makes the whole aggregate unknown
options.why: That is how NULL behaves in *scalar* expressions (`1 + NULL` really is NULL) but aggregates deliberately break that rule and skip nulls instead. Knowing that aggregates are the exception is most of the point of this question.

options.text: 3, 2 and 1.5: aggregates skip NULLs, so the average divided by 2 rather than 3
options.why: `count(*)` counts rows, `count(v)` counts non-NULL values, and `avg` sums 3 over 2 values. Whether 1.5 is right depends entirely on what the NULL meant. "Sensor offline" makes it the correct average of known readings; "we failed to record a zero" makes it a 50% overstatement. The database cannot distinguish the two cases, and neither can anything downstream of it.

options.text: 3, 3 and 1.0: NULL counts as zero in numeric aggregates
options.why: This is the intuition the behaviour is designed to contradict. NULL is not zero; it is unknown. Treating it as zero would mean claiming knowledge you do not have, so SQL leaves it out of the calculation entirely.

quiz.prompt: Name a place where SQL treats two NULLs as equal to each other, and a place where it treats them as not equal.

options.text: Equality depends on the column's type; numeric NULLs compare equal, text NULLs do not
options.why: Type has nothing to do with it. The behaviour differs by *clause* (GROUP BY versus WHERE) and is identical for every data type.

options.text: `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT` put all NULLs together; `WHERE v = NULL` and a plain `UNIQUE` constraint treat them as never equal
options.why: Both halves are real and they contradict each other inside one language. Two NULL rows collapse into a single group, yet `WHERE v = NULL` matches neither of them, and a UNIQUE column will happily accept both. `ORDER BY` takes a third position: Postgres sorts NULLs as larger than everything, hence NULLS FIRST as an option. This inconsistency is what the long-running theoretical argument about nulls is actually about.

options.text: They are equal everywhere except inside aggregate functions
options.why: Backwards on the main point, and aggregates are not doing an equality comparison at all: they simply exclude NULL inputs before computing anything.

options.text: They are never treated as equal anywhere; that is the single consistent rule
options.why: It would be a much easier language if that were true. Run `GROUP BY v` on a table with two NULL rows and you get one group of two, which is only possible if something decided those NULLs were the same.

quiz.prompt: A `UNIQUE` column in PostgreSQL already contains a NULL. You insert another NULL. What happens, and how would you make it fail instead?

options.text: It is accepted (uniqueness is defined by equality and NULLs are never equal) and `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` makes the second one fail
options.why: You can insert as many NULLs into a UNIQUE column as you like, which is correct by the rules and almost never what the person reading the schema expects. PostgreSQL 15 added NULLS NOT DISTINCT to say "for this constraint, treat unknowns as equal"; before that the options were NOT NULL or a partial unique index. It took about thirty years for the language to offer the choice.

options.text: It is accepted, but only because the column is nullable; a NOT NULL column would compare NULLs as equal
options.why: A NOT NULL column cannot contain a NULL at all, so there is nothing there to compare. Nullability governs whether NULLs may be stored, never how they compare once stored.

options.text: It is rejected: a unique constraint permits at most one NULL
options.why: That is SQL Server's behaviour, and assuming it is portable is how this bug crosses engines. The SQL standard, and PostgreSQL with it, allows any number of NULLs in a unique column by default.

options.text: It is accepted, and there is no way to forbid it short of `NOT NULL`
options.why: Right about the acceptance, out of date on the remedy. NOT NULL is one answer, but `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PostgreSQL 15+) forbids the duplicate NULL while still permitting a single one, and a partial unique index solved it before that.

hooks.remember: `NULL = NULL` is unknown, not true, and `WHERE` keeps only rows whose condition is true.
hooks.hook: NULL is a **sealed envelope**. Is this envelope equal to that one? Nobody knows: unknown. *Not* equal? Also unknown. Only `IS NULL` asks a question with an answer: "is this an envelope?". And `WHERE` is a bouncer who admits only a definite **yes**. Unknown is thrown out with false, without a word.

hooks.remember: One NULL in the list makes `x NOT IN (…)` return no rows for every `x`; use `NOT EXISTS`.
hooks.hook: `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` is `x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL`. That last term is an envelope, so the whole `AND` can never become true. **One drop of NULL poisons the well**, and every row, for every possible `x`, is turned away. The antidote is `NOT EXISTS`, which asks about *rows*, and a row either exists or it does not.

hooks.remember: Aggregates skip NULLs: `count(*)` counts rows, `count(v)` non-NULL values, `avg` divides by the latter.
hooks.hook: Aggregates are terribly polite: they pretend NULLs are **not in the room**. `count(*)` counts the people. `count(v)` counts the people who answered. `avg` divides by those who answered, so 1, 2 and a NULL average to **1.5**, not 1. Whether that is right depends on what the silence meant, and the database cannot ask.

hooks.remember: Two NULLs are unequal in WHERE but grouped together by GROUP BY and DISTINCT, and UNIQUE lets any number in.
hooks.hook: NULL is two-faced, and this sentence sorts its faces: **W**here **W**on't match, **G**roup **G**athers, **U**nique is **U**nlimited, **O**rder puts them **O**ut last (ascending). `UNIQUE` admits a hundred NULLs because its rule is "same value?", and envelopes are never the same. `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PostgreSQL 15) tells it: one envelope only.

Write every result you saw into the file as a comment beside the query that produced it,
so step 2 and step 4 sit side by side.

the failing condition expanded term by term, with the unknown one identified
