days.title: Joins multiply
days.teaser: Revenue nearly quadrupled overnight, and nobody sold anything
days.teachBack: An order with three items and two payments is joined to both tables, and the report shows six times its total. Explain where each of the six rows comes from, why `sum(DISTINCT amount)` is not a fix, and how restructuring the query makes every number right.
days.theoryMarkdown:
## One side repeats once per match

In day 5 a join *lost* rows without a word. Here it makes extra ones, which is worse,
because extra rows go straight into sums, and inflated sums look like good news. Nobody
files a bug when revenue goes up.

```sql
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS day06 CASCADE;
CREATE SCHEMA day06;
SET search_path = day06;

CREATE TABLE orders   (id int PRIMARY KEY, customer text NOT NULL, total numeric(10,2) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE items    (order_id int REFERENCES orders, sku text NOT NULL, qty int NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE payments (order_id int REFERENCES orders, amount numeric(10,2) NOT NULL);

INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'ana', 100.00), (2, 'bo', 80.00);
INSERT INTO items VALUES (1, 'mug', 1), (1, 'tea', 2), (1, 'spoon', 1), (2, 'kettle', 1);
INSERT INTO payments VALUES (1, 50.00), (1, 50.00), (2, 80.00);
```

Two orders. `ana` bought three things for 100.00 and paid in two halves, which is a
perfectly ordinary split payment. `bo` bought a kettle for 80.00 and paid once. The truth,
straight from each table:

```sql
SELECT (SELECT sum(total) FROM orders) AS revenue, (SELECT sum(amount) FROM payments) AS paid;
```

```text
 revenue |  paid
---------+--------
  180.00 | 180.00
```

### A join repeats the "one" side once per match on the "many" side

Join orders to items and sum the order totals:

```sql
SELECT sum(o.total) FROM orders o JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.id;
```

```text
  sum
--------
 380.00
```

Nothing is broken here. The join did exactly what joins do. `ana`'s order matched three
item rows, so it appears three times, and its 100.00 is summed three times:
`3 × 100 + 1 × 80 = 380`. In one-to-many terms, the "one" side (an order) is repeated once
for every match on the "many" side (its items). This is called **fan-out**.

### Two "many" sides multiply

Now the report someone actually asked for: per customer, revenue, amount paid, and number
of line items. One query, two joins:

```sql
SELECT o.customer,
       sum(o.total)  AS revenue,
       sum(p.amount) AS paid,
       count(i.sku)  AS lines
FROM orders o
JOIN items    i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer
ORDER BY o.customer;
```

```text
 customer | revenue |  paid  | lines
----------+---------+--------+-------
 ana      |  600.00 | 300.00 |     6
 bo       |   80.00 |  80.00 |     1
```

`ana`'s 100.00 order shows as 600.00 in revenue, 300.00 paid, and 6 lines. `bo` is right,
and only by luck: one item and one payment, so nothing multiplied. That is how this bug
survives testing. Every simple test case comes out right.

Look at the rows the aggregates actually saw:

```sql
SELECT o.id, i.sku, p.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN items    i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
ORDER BY o.id, i.sku, p.amount;
```

```text
 id |  sku   | amount
----+--------+--------
  1 | mug    |  50.00
  1 | mug    |  50.00
  1 | spoon  |  50.00
  1 | spoon  |  50.00
  1 | tea    |  50.00
  1 | tea    |  50.00
  2 | kettle |  80.00
```

Items and payments have nothing to do with each other. They are both about the order,
not about each other, so the join paired **every item with every payment**: 3 × 2 = 6 rows
for order 1. Revenue counted the order once per row (×6). Payments were counted once per
item (×3). Items were counted once per payment (×2). Three different wrong numbers, each
off by a different factor.

## Seeing it, and naming it

Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day06;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and reports how many rows each node actually produced,
which makes fan-out visible without guessing:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT sum(o.total)
FROM orders o
JOIN items    i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id;
```

```text
                                 QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate (actual rows=1 loops=1)
   ->  Hash Join (actual rows=7 loops=1)
         Hash Cond: (i.order_id = o.id)
         ->  Seq Scan on items i (actual rows=4 loops=1)
         ->  Hash (actual rows=3 loops=1)
               Buckets: 2048  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 17kB
               ->  Hash Join (actual rows=3 loops=1)
                     Hash Cond: (p.order_id = o.id)
                     ->  Seq Scan on payments p (actual rows=3 loops=1)
                     ->  Hash (actual rows=2 loops=1)
                           Buckets: 1024  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 9kB
                           ->  Seq Scan on orders o (actual rows=2 loops=1)
```

Read it bottom-up again: 2 orders come in, 3 rows leave the first join, 7 leave the
second. Two orders fed the aggregate seven rows. On a real table this is the number to look
at, and when a join's output is larger than the row count of the table you meant to
report on, you have fan-out. (Your `Memory Usage` figures may differ slightly. The `rows=`
numbers will not.)

### Grain: what one row means

The idea that prevents all of this has a name from data warehousing: **grain**. The grain of
a result is what one row of it *stands for*. Ralph Kimball's four-step design process
puts "declare the grain" second, right after choosing the business process. His group's
writing calls failing to declare it up front the most frequent design error.

Apply it to the report. The intended grain is **one row per customer**. `orders` has a grain
of one row per order. `items` has one row per order line. `payments` has one row per
payment. Joining tables of different grains produces a result whose grain is *their
combination*, here one row per (line, payment) pair, and summing anything at that grain
counts it once per pair.

So the rule: **bring each table to the grain of the report before you join it.**

## Aggregate first, join second

Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day06;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

Collapse `items` and `payments` to one row per order each. Now every join is one-to-one,
and nothing can multiply:

```sql
SELECT o.customer, o.total AS revenue, p.paid, i.lines
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT order_id, count(*) AS lines FROM items GROUP BY order_id) i
  ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) p
  ON p.order_id = o.id
ORDER BY o.customer;
```

```text
 customer | revenue |  paid  | lines
----------+---------+--------+-------
 ana      |  100.00 | 100.00 |     3
 bo       |   80.00 |  80.00 |     1
```

Every number is right. The same idea written as correlated subqueries, one per measure, is
often easier to read and just as correct:

```sql
SELECT o.customer, o.total AS revenue,
       (SELECT sum(amount) FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id) AS paid,
       (SELECT count(*)    FROM items    i WHERE i.order_id = o.id) AS lines
FROM orders o
ORDER BY o.customer;
```

```text
 customer | revenue |  paid  | lines
----------+---------+--------+-------
 ana      |  100.00 | 100.00 |     3
 bo       |   80.00 |  80.00 |     1
```

Either form keeps the grain honest. A customer with several orders would need one more
`GROUP BY customer` on top. The principle does not change: aggregate the "many" side
before it meets anything else.

### The tempting fix that loses money

`count(DISTINCT x)` is a correct way to count things that a join duplicated. So it is
natural to reach for `DISTINCT` everywhere:

```sql
SELECT o.customer,
       sum(DISTINCT o.total)  AS revenue,
       sum(DISTINCT p.amount) AS paid,
       count(DISTINCT i.sku)  AS lines
FROM orders o
JOIN items    i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer
ORDER BY o.customer;
```

```text
 customer | revenue | paid  | lines
----------+---------+-------+-------
 ana      |  100.00 | 50.00 |     3
 bo       |   80.00 | 80.00 |     1
```

Revenue and lines now look right, and `paid` is **50.00**. `ana` made two payments of
exactly 50.00, and `sum(DISTINCT amount)` adds each *distinct value* once. Two real
payments of the same size are, to `DISTINCT`, the same number. The revenue column only
looks right by coincidence. Give `ana` a second order that also totals 100.00 and it
collapses the same way. Even `count(DISTINCT i.sku)` would break the day someone orders
the same SKU on two lines. `DISTINCT` removes equal *values*. What you needed to remove was
duplicated *rows*, and rows are identified by keys, not by what they happen to contain.

## A famous bug, and a one-line detector

Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day06;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

### Tools that ship a fix for it

This exact problem is common enough that tools ship features against it:

- **Looker** calls it "fanout" and has a feature named *symmetric aggregates*. When a model
  declares a join as one-to-many, Looker rewrites `sum` so that each value is counted once
  per *primary key* rather than once per row. Its documentation describes it as on by
  default. It is the `DISTINCT` idea done properly, keyed on identity instead of value.
- **Entity Framework Core** documents it as *cartesian explosion*: loading a blog with
  both its posts and its tags in one query returns posts × tags rows. Its answer,
  `AsSplitQuery()`, sends one query per collection instead.
- **Hibernate** refuses outright. Ask it to fetch two list-type collections of one entity
  in one query and it throws `MultipleBagFetchException: cannot simultaneously fetch
  multiple bags`, because the result would be exactly the 3 × 2 table above.

All three treat two independent one-to-many joins in one query as almost never what
anyone meant.

### Worth knowing: a one-line fan-out detector

Before trusting any join you are about to aggregate, compare the number of rows with the
number of distinct keys at the grain you meant:

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS rows, count(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN items    i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id;
```

```text
 rows | orders
------+--------
    7 |      2
```

If they differ, every `sum` over that join is suspect. And checking the assumption that a
relationship is one-to-one, rather than believing it, is a single query:

```sql
SELECT order_id, count(*) FROM payments GROUP BY order_id HAVING count(*) > 1;
```

```text
 order_id | count
----------+-------
        1 |     2
```

Somebody once said "each order has one payment", the schema never enforced it, and here
is the order that proves otherwise. If the relationship really must be one-to-one, a
`UNIQUE` constraint on `payments.order_id` would make the database refuse the second row,
and then it would be safe to rely on.

### Carry this

- A join repeats the "one" side once per match on the "many" side. Two independent
  "many" sides multiply.
- Decide the grain of the result first: what does one row mean?
- Aggregate each "many" table down to the report's grain *before* joining it.
- `count(DISTINCT key)` can repair a count. `sum(DISTINCT value)` cannot repair a sum.
- If a join's row count exceeds the distinct count of the keys you are reporting on, stop
  and look.

```text
        1 |     2
```

Somebody once said "each order has one payment", the schema never enforced it, and here
is the order that proves otherwise. If the relationship really must be one-to-one, a
`UNIQUE` constraint on `payments.order_id` would make the database refuse the second row,
and then it would be safe to rely on.

### Carry this

- A join repeats the "one" side once per match on the "many" side. Two independent
  "many" sides multiply.
- Decide the grain of the result first: what does one row mean?
- Aggregate each "many" table down to the report's grain *before* joining it.
- `count(DISTINCT key)` can repair a count. `sum(DISTINCT value)` cannot repair a sum.
- If a join's row count exceeds the distinct count of the keys you are reporting on, stop
  and look.

drill.code:
SELECT o.customer,
       sum(o.total)  AS revenue,
       sum(p.amount) AS paid,
       count(i.sku)  AS lines
FROM orders o
JOIN items    i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer;
drill.prompt: Order 3 belongs to `cy`, totals 40.00, has 2 item rows, and was paid in 4 payments of 10.00. What does this report show for `cy`?

options.text: revenue 240.00, paid 60.00, lines 6
options.why: That treats the join as 2 + 4 = 6 rows. Joins multiply, they don't add.

options.text: revenue 40.00, paid 40.00, lines 2
options.why: The truth, and what a pre-aggregated version returns. With both children joined directly, the order becomes 8 rows before anything is summed.

options.text: revenue 160.00, paid 40.00, lines 4
options.why: That is fan-out from the payments join alone. The items join multiplies it a second time.

options.text: revenue 320.00, paid 80.00, lines 8
options.why: 2 items × 4 payments = 8 rows. The total is on every row (40 × 8 = 320), each payment appears once per item (40 × 2 = 80), and each item once per payment (2 × 4 = 8). Each column is wrong by a different factor, which is why one "looks a bit high" check never catches it.

drill.code:
SELECT o.id, count(DISTINCT i.sku) AS lines
FROM orders o
JOIN items    i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id;
drill.prompt: Order 4 has two item rows, both for `mug` (qty 1 and qty 2), and two payments of 15.00. The fan-out was "fixed" with `count(DISTINCT i.sku)`. What does it report?

options.text: 1: the two `mug` lines share a SKU, so DISTINCT merges them
options.why: `count(DISTINCT sku)` counts distinct *products*, not lines. It looked like a fix only because every earlier order happened to use different SKUs. To count lines you need something that identifies a line (a line id) or to count the items table before joining.

options.text: It fails, because DISTINCT cannot be combined with GROUP BY
options.why: Aggregate DISTINCT and GROUP BY combine freely. It runs, which is the problem.

options.text: 4: DISTINCT has no effect inside an aggregate
options.why: It has an effect, and here too much of one: 4 joined rows, 1 distinct SKU.

options.text: 2: DISTINCT removes the payment duplication and keeps both lines
options.why: DISTINCT inside count looks only at the value `sku`. It cannot tell a duplicated row from a second, genuine line with the same SKU.

drill.code:
-- A
SELECT o.customer, sum(p.amount) FROM orders o
JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer;

-- B
SELECT o.customer, sum(DISTINCT p.amount) FROM orders o
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer;

-- C
SELECT o.customer, sum(p.amount) FROM orders o
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.customer;
drill.prompt: `ana` has two orders (100.00 paid as 50 + 50, and 60.00 paid once); `bo` has one (80.00, paid once). Order 1 also has 3 items. Which queries report `ana`'s total paid as 160.00?

options.text: B and C
options.why: B has no fan-out to fix and still breaks: ana's distinct payment amounts are 50 and 60, so it reports 110.00.

options.text: A and C
options.why: A joins items as well, which turns order 1's two payments into six rows: 300 + 60 = 360.00.

options.text: C only
options.why: C joins one "many" table and sums that table's own column. Each payment row appears exactly once, so the sum is right; only the order columns repeat, and C does not sum them. A gives 360.00, because the items join triples order 1's payments. B gives 110.00: the distinct amounts are 50 and 60, so one real 50 is lost.

options.text: None: any join to payments inflates the payment total
options.why: A one-to-many join repeats the "one" side, not the "many" side. Summing a column of the many side, with no other many-side join, counts each of its rows once.

challenges.prompt: One row per customer, with `customer`, `revenue` (the order total), `paid` (the sum of their payments) and `lines` (their item rows): every number correct, not multiplied by the other table. Ordered by customer.
challenges.solution:
SELECT o.customer, o.total AS revenue, p.paid, i.lines
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT order_id, count(*) AS lines FROM items GROUP BY order_id) i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) p ON p.order_id = o.id
ORDER BY o.customer;
challenges.hint: Reduce each many-side table to one row per order before it meets anything else.

challenges.prompt: Join `orders` to both `items` and `payments`, and return two numbers in one row: how many rows the join produced, and how many distinct orders are in it.
challenges.solution:
SELECT count(*) AS rows, count(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id;
challenges.hint: Compare a plain count with a count of distinct keys over the same join.

challenges.prompt: Which orders have more than one payment? Return `order_id` and the number of payments.
challenges.solution:
SELECT order_id, count(*) AS payments
FROM payments
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING count(*) > 1;
challenges.hint: Group, then filter the groups.

challenges.prompt: From `items`, return in one row `multi`, how many lines have `qty` above 1, and `all_lines`, how many lines there are in total, without joining or using a subquery.
challenges.solution: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE qty > 1) AS multi, count(*) AS all_lines FROM items;
challenges.hint: An aggregate can carry its own filter.

quiz.prompt: An order totalling 100.00 has three item rows. Why does `SELECT sum(o.total) FROM orders o JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.id` count it as 300.00?

options.text: It is a bug in `sum` over joined tables that `GROUP BY` would fix
options.why: `sum` faithfully adds up the rows it is given. Grouping by order would give one group per order: still containing three rows each, still summing to 300.

options.text: The join produces one row per item, and each of those rows carries the order's total, so the sum sees it three times
options.why: This is fan-out: the "one" side of a one-to-many join is repeated once per match on the "many" side. The join is not wrong: summing a column from the repeated side at that grain is.

options.text: Postgres double-counts numeric columns across joins unless they are indexed
options.why: Indexes affect how rows are found, never which rows exist. The three rows are the correct output of that join.

options.text: The items' quantities are being multiplied into the total
options.why: `qty` never enters the query. The factor is the number of item rows, whatever their quantities are.

quiz.prompt: One order has 3 items and 2 payments. When both tables are joined to it in one query, how many rows does that order become, and why?

options.text: 6: every item is paired with every payment, because neither table relates to the other except through the order
options.why: Two independent one-to-many joins multiply: 3 × 2. Every aggregate over that result is wrong by a different factor: the order total ×6, payments ×3, item counts ×2.

options.text: 2: the join stops at the smaller table
options.why: No join type works that way. Row counts in an inner join come only from which pairings satisfy ON.

options.text: 3: the larger of the two child tables decides the row count
options.why: That would require pairing each payment with only some items. Nothing in the ON conditions says which item a payment belongs to, so every pairing is kept.

options.text: 5: three item rows plus two payment rows
options.why: Joins do not stack rows side by side like a UNION. Each output row combines one item and one payment for the same order, and all combinations survive the ON conditions.

quiz.prompt: A report joins orders to both items and payments and shows inflated payment totals. Why is changing `sum(p.amount)` to `sum(DISTINCT p.amount)` not a fix?

options.text: It is a correct fix but too slow for large tables
options.why: Speed is not the problem; correctness is. It returns the wrong total whenever two genuine payments share an amount.

options.text: DISTINCT applies to the whole row, so it removes nothing
options.why: Inside an aggregate, DISTINCT applies only to that aggregate's argument. That is exactly why it collapses equal amounts.

options.text: `sum(DISTINCT …)` is not valid SQL
options.why: It is valid, which is what makes it dangerous: it runs and returns a plausible number.

options.text: DISTINCT removes equal *values*, not duplicated *rows*, so two real payments of the same amount are counted once
options.why: A split payment of 50 + 50 becomes 50. Rows are identified by keys, not by what they contain. The real fix is to aggregate payments per order before joining, so nothing is duplicated in the first place.

quiz.prompt: What does "the grain of a result" mean, and what rule about grain prevents fan-out?

options.text: The level of detail of a column's data type, like `numeric(10,2)`
options.why: Grain is about rows, not values: what a single row means. Precision is a different thing.

options.text: What one row of the result stands for; bring every table to the report's grain (aggregate it) before joining it
options.why: If the report is one row per customer, items and payments must be reduced to one row per order or per customer first. Then every join is one-to-one and nothing can multiply. Kimball's design process puts declaring the grain second, right after choosing the business process.

options.text: The number of rows in a table; join the smallest tables first
options.why: Join order is the planner's job and does not change the result. Fan-out comes from joining tables whose rows mean different things.

options.text: The primary key of each table; always select it
options.why: Keys help you *detect* the grain, but selecting them changes nothing. What matters is aggregating down to the intended grain before joining.

quiz.prompt: How can `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` show you that a join has fanned out?

options.text: It prints a warning line when a join duplicates rows
options.why: There is no such warning. Fan-out is legitimate join behaviour; only you know that you did not want it.

options.text: It shows `Fanout: true` on the join node
options.why: No such field exists. You infer fan-out from the `rows=` numbers.

options.text: It reports the actual row count of every node, so you can see a join emitting more rows than there are entities you meant to report on
options.why: Two orders entering and seven rows leaving the join is fan-out you can read directly off the plan. A quick confirmation is to compare count(*) with count(DISTINCT key) over the same join.

options.text: It cannot: fan-out is only visible in the final result
options.why: EXPLAIN ANALYZE's `actual rows` is the clearest place to see it, node by node, before any aggregate has hidden it.

quiz.prompt: A report joins `orders` to `items` and to `payments` and every total is inflated. Why does collapsing `items` and `payments` to one row per order *before* the join make every total right?

options.text: Subqueries in `FROM` are evaluated separately, so their rows are never joined
options.why: They are joined like any table. What changed is that they now have one row per order, so the join has nothing to multiply.

options.text: Each join becomes one-to-one, so no order row is repeated and nothing is counted more than once
options.why: Fan-out happens when a row meets several matches. Bring each side to the report's grain first (one row per order) and every pairing is one row with one row.

options.text: Grouping removes duplicate values, the same thing `DISTINCT` does
options.why: `GROUP BY order_id` collapses rows by *key*: two payments of 50.00 are added, not merged as one value. That is exactly the difference from `DISTINCT`.

quiz.prompt: Before trusting a `sum` over a join meant to be one row per order, which two counts do you compare to see whether the join fanned out?

options.text: `sum(o.total)` against `sum(DISTINCT o.total)`
options.why: Two different orders can have the same total, so the distinct sum can be wrong even when nothing fanned out. Count keys, not values.

options.text: `count(*)` of the joined rows against `count(DISTINCT o.id)`
options.why: At the grain you meant, every order is one row, so the two are equal. If the join produced more rows than distinct orders, something repeated them, and every sum over it is suspect.

options.text: `count(*)` of `orders` against `count(*)` of `items`
options.why: Those are always different when orders have several items, and say nothing about what a particular join did.

quiz.prompt: Someone says "each order has exactly one payment". How do you check it, and how would you make the database guarantee it?

options.text: Join the two tables and check that nothing errors
options.why: A join never errors on duplicates. It multiplies without a word, and that is the problem.

options.text: Check that `payments.order_id` has a foreign key to `orders`; the foreign key guarantees one payment per order
options.why: A foreign key says each payment points at a real order. Any number of payments may point at the same one.

options.text: `SELECT order_id, count(*) FROM payments GROUP BY order_id HAVING count(*) > 1` lists the exceptions; a `UNIQUE` constraint on `payments.order_id` prevents them
options.why: An assumption the schema does not enforce is a guess. The query finds the orders that break it; the constraint makes the database refuse the second payment, and only then is it safe to rely on.

hooks.remember: A join repeats the "one" side once per match; two independent "many" sides multiply.
hooks.hook: Joins breed like **rabbits**. An order joined to its 3 items becomes 3 copies of the order. Add its 2 payments in the same query and every item pairs with every payment: **3 × 2 = 6** copies, each carrying the full 100.00. Revenue looks fantastic, and nobody files a bug when revenue goes up.

hooks.remember: Decide the grain (what one row means) first, and bring every table to it before joining.
hooks.hook: **Grain** is the answer to "what does one row stand for?". Orders are one per order, items one per line, payments one per payment. Stir them together and you get flour of **one row per (line, payment)**, which is nobody's report. Name the report's grain out loud ("one row per customer") before you write a single join.

hooks.remember: Aggregate each "many" table to the report's grain before joining; `sum(DISTINCT)` is not a fix.
hooks.hook: **Boil each "many" table down** to one row per order first, then join one-to-one and nothing can multiply. Do not reach for `sum(DISTINCT amount)`: two honest payments of 50 look like *one* 50 to DISTINCT, which removes equal **values**, not duplicate **rows**. Rows are told apart by keys, not by what they happen to contain.

hooks.remember: Before summing over a join, compare `count(*)` with `count(DISTINCT key)` at the grain you meant.
hooks.hook: A two-number **smoke alarm**: `count(*)` and `count(DISTINCT o.id)` over the join you are about to sum. Same number? Quiet. Different? Something is breeding. And "each order has one payment" is a belief until a `GROUP BY order_id HAVING count(*) > 1` finds the order that disagrees, or a `UNIQUE` constraint makes it law.

days.title: Without ORDER BY there is no order
days.teaser: The leaderboard that changed its mind when someone added an index
days.teachBack: Explain why page 2 of an `OFFSET`-paginated feed can show a post that was already on page 1, and why a deep `OFFSET` stays slow even with a perfect index. Then explain what keyset pagination remembers instead, and why the tiebreaker column is not optional.
days.theoryMarkdown:
## A table is a heap, not a list

Run a `SELECT` without `ORDER BY` on a small table and the rows come back in the order you
inserted them. Run it a thousand times and they come back the same way a thousand times.
So code starts to rely on it: the "first" row, the "latest" entry, page 2 of a list. This
lesson is about why that order is an accident of how the rows happen to be stored and
read, and the three different ways the accident ends.

```sql
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS day07 CASCADE;
CREATE SCHEMA day07;
SET search_path = day07;

CREATE TABLE players (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, score int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO players VALUES (1, 'ana', 90), (2, 'bo', 75), (3, 'cy', 90), (4, 'dee', 60), (5, 'eli', 75);
SELECT * FROM players;
```

```text
 id | name | score
----+------+-------
  1 | ana  |    90
  2 | bo   |    75
  3 | cy   |    90
  4 | dee  |    60
  5 | eli  |    75
```

### A table is a heap, not a list

The SQL standard is blunt: without `ORDER BY`, the order of rows is *implementation
dependent*. The relational model is blunter. A relation is a **set**, and sets have no
order at all. What you just saw is simply the order in which a sequential scan meets the
rows in the table's pages, and on day 1 you saw what an `UPDATE` does to a row: it writes
a new version, somewhere else.

```sql
UPDATE players SET score = 91 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT ctid, * FROM players;
```

```text
 ctid  | id | name | score
-------+----+------+-------
 (0,2) |  2 | bo   |    75
 (0,3) |  3 | cy   |    90
 (0,4) |  4 | dee  |    60
 (0,5) |  5 | eli  |    75
 (0,6) |  1 | ana  |    91
```

`ana` was first. One update later, `ana` is last. Nobody touched the query. The new version
of the row went into the next free slot on the page, `(0,6)`, and the scan meets it there.
On a busy table the same thing happens through updates, deletes, `VACUUM` freeing space
mid-table, and bulk loads, all day long. "Insertion order" holds only until the first
write.

```sql
UPDATE players SET score = 90 WHERE id = 1;
```

## Ties are unordered too

Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day07;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

### ORDER BY with ties is unordered too

This is the version that gets past people who know the first rule. You did write
`ORDER BY`. `ana` and `cy` both have 90:

```sql
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 cy   |    90
 ana  |    90
```

`ORDER BY score` promises an order between different scores. Between equal scores it
promises nothing. Watch what an index does to that "nothing". On a tiny table the planner
would not bother with an index, so for the experiment, discourage sequential scans:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON players (score);
SET enable_seqscan = off;
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2;
RESET enable_seqscan;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 ana  |    90
 cy   |    90
```

Same data, same query, and a different winner. The first plan read the heap and sorted it,
and `cy` came out on top. The second walked the index backwards, and the index stores
equal keys in its own order. On a real table you do not set anything: the planner switches
plans by itself when the statistics change, after an `ANALYZE`, a bit of growth, or a
version upgrade. Your leaderboard changes its mind and nobody deployed anything.

The fix is to make the order **total**. Add a column that is unique as the last sort key,
so no two rows can ever tie:

```sql
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC, id LIMIT 3;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 ana  |    90
 cy   |    90
 bo   |    75
```

And when ties should *share* a place instead of being broken arbitrarily, Postgres 13
added the standard way to say so:

```sql
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 cy   |    90
 ana  |    90
 bo   |    75
 eli  |    75
```

Asked for three, got four. The third place is a tie between `bo` and `eli`, and
`WITH TIES` refuses to pick one for you.

## Paging with OFFSET

Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day07;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

The textbook way to page through a list:

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  title      text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO posts (created_at, title)
SELECT timestamptz '2026-01-01' + n * interval '1 minute', 'post ' || n
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS n;
CREATE INDEX posts_feed ON posts (created_at DESC, id DESC);
VACUUM ANALYZE posts;

SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3;
```

```text
   id   |    title
--------+-------------
 100000 | post 100000
  99999 | post 99999
  99998 | post 99998
```

That is page 1. While the reader looks at it, somebody publishes a post. Then the reader
clicks "next":

```sql
INSERT INTO posts (created_at, title) VALUES (timestamptz '2026-12-31', 'breaking news');
SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
```

```text
  id   |   title
-------+------------
 99998 | post 99998
 99997 | post 99997
 99996 | post 99996
```

`post 99998` again. `OFFSET 3` means "skip three rows", not "skip the three you saw", and
the new post pushed everything down by one. A delete does the opposite and silently skips a
row. Every infinite-scroll feed built on `OFFSET` has this bug, and on a busy feed it fires
constantly.

### And OFFSET is slow, however good the index

The second problem is cost. `OFFSET` takes a number, and the only thing a database can do
with a number is count. To skip 90,000 rows it has to produce 90,000 rows and throw them
away:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 90000;
```

```text
                               QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Limit (actual rows=10 loops=1)
   ->  Index Scan using posts_feed on posts (actual rows=90010 loops=1)
```

The index scan did its job perfectly, and walked 90,010 entries to hand back 10. Page 9,001
costs nine thousand times what page 1 costs. Users rarely go that deep, but crawlers,
exports and "load all" buttons do.

## Keyset pagination

Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day07;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

Instead of remembering *how many* rows you have seen, remember *the last one*. Each page
asks for the rows that come after it in the sort order. With a two-column sort, "after" is
a comparison of the pair, and SQL has exactly that, a **row comparison**:

```sql
SELECT id, title FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-07 22:42:00+00', 10002)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

```text
  id   |   title
-------+------------
 10001 | post 10001
 10000 | post 10000
  9999 | post 9999
```

`(a, b) < (x, y)` means `a < x OR (a = x AND b < y)`, which is "earlier, or at the same
moment with a smaller id". Since the index is on exactly `(created_at, id)`, Postgres can
jump straight to that position:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT id, title FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-07 22:42:00+00', 10002)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

```text
                                                 QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Limit (actual rows=10 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=4
   ->  Index Scan using posts_feed on posts (actual rows=10 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (ROW(created_at, id) < ROW('2026-01-07 22:42:00+00'::timestamp with time zone, 10002))
         Buffers: shared hit=4
```

Ten rows read for ten rows returned. Run the `OFFSET 90000` query with `BUFFERS` added and
compare: whether your numbers say `hit`, `read` or both depends on what is cached, but
their total for the offset version is around a thousand pages, against about four here. A
new post at the top cannot shift this page either, because it is anchored to a row, not to
a count.

Markus Winand, author of *Use The Index, Luke*, has campaigned for years under the banner
"No Offset", and many large public APIs page this way. Stripe's list endpoints take
`starting_after=<object id>` rather than a page number. The trade-off is that
keyset pagination cannot jump to "page 37". It moves forwards and backwards from where you
are. For feeds, timelines, exports and APIs that is exactly what you want. For a search
results page with numbered links, people still use `OFFSET` and accept the cost.

### The keyset that looks right and skips rows

To see why the row comparison matters, take a small feed where two posts share a
timestamp and one was imported late with a backdated time, so `id` and `created_at`
disagree:

```sql
CREATE TABLE feed (id int PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL, title text);
INSERT INTO feed VALUES
  (1, '2026-05-01 10:00+00', 'first'),
  (2, '2026-05-01 10:05+00', 'second'),
  (3, '2026-05-01 10:05+00', 'third'),
  (4, '2026-05-01 10:10+00', 'fourth'),
  (5, '2026-05-01 10:02+00', 'imported late');
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM feed ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 id |       created_at       | title
----+------------------------+--------
  4 | 2026-05-01 10:10:00+00 | fourth
  3 | 2026-05-01 10:05:00+00 | third
```

Page 1 ended at `(10:05, 3)`. The tempting way to write "after that" compares each column
separately:

```sql
SELECT id, title FROM feed
WHERE created_at < '2026-05-01 10:05+00' AND id < 3
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 id | title
----+-------
  1 | first
```

`second` is lost because it shares the timestamp, and `imported late` is lost because its
id is larger. The row comparison gets both:

```sql
SELECT id, title FROM feed
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-05-01 10:05+00', 3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 id |     title
----+---------------
  2 | second
  5 | imported late
```

## The same query can start in the middle

Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day07;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

### Worth knowing: the same query can start in the middle of the table

One more way order goes away, and it involves nobody's writes at all. Since 8.3, Postgres
has **synchronized sequential scans**. When one scan is already reading through a big
table, a second one starts wherever the first one currently is, wraps around at the end,
and the two share their disk reads. "Big" means larger than a quarter of `shared_buffers`,
so on a default install anything above 32 MB. You can watch it happen in a single session:

```sql
CREATE TABLE big AS
SELECT g AS id, repeat('x', 200) AS pad FROM generate_series(1, 300000) AS g;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('big')) AS size, current_setting('shared_buffers');

SELECT id FROM big LIMIT 3;
```

```text
 size  | current_setting
-------+-----------------
 69 MB | 128MB
```

```text
 id
----
  1
  2
  3
```

Now leave a scan partway through, with a cursor that skips 100,000 rows and stops:

```sql order
BEGIN;
DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT id FROM big;
MOVE 100000 IN c;
COMMIT;
```

Then ask for "the first three rows" again:

```sql
SELECT id FROM big LIMIT 3;
```

```text
  id
-------
 99553
 99554
 99555
```

The same `SELECT id FROM big LIMIT 3`, a second later, starts near row 100,000. Scans
report their position every 16 pages, so your number will be a little below 100,000 rather
than exactly this one. Turn the feature off and it goes back to the beginning:

```sql
SET synchronize_seqscans = off;
SELECT id FROM big LIMIT 3;
RESET synchronize_seqscans;
DROP TABLE big;
```

```text
 id
----
  1
  2
  3
```

The manual warns that this "can result in unpredictable changes in the row ordering
returned by queries that have no ORDER BY clause", and Franck Pachot has written up the
`LIMIT`-without-`ORDER BY` version of exactly this experiment. It shows directly that the
order you saw was never a property of the table.

### Carry this

- No `ORDER BY`, no order. Not "insertion order", not "probably the same".
- `ORDER BY` is only as deterministic as its last key. End it with something unique, such
  as the primary key.
- Use `FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES` when ties should share a place.
- `OFFSET` duplicates and skips under concurrent writes, and costs as many rows as it
  skips.
- Keyset pagination: `WHERE (sort_col, id) < (last_sort_col, last_id)`, an index on
  exactly those columns, and never two separate `<` comparisons.

parts.title: A table is a heap, not a list
parts.markdown:
Run a `SELECT` without `ORDER BY` on a small table and the rows come back in the order you
inserted them. Run it a thousand times and they come back the same way a thousand times.
So code starts to rely on it: the "first" row, the "latest" entry, page 2 of a list. This
lesson is about why that order is an accident of how the rows happen to be stored and
read, and the three different ways the accident ends.

```sql
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS day07 CASCADE;
CREATE SCHEMA day07;
SET search_path = day07;

CREATE TABLE players (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, score int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO players VALUES (1, 'ana', 90), (2, 'bo', 75), (3, 'cy', 90), (4, 'dee', 60), (5, 'eli', 75);
SELECT * FROM players;
```

```text
 id | name | score
----+------+-------
  1 | ana  |    90
  2 | bo   |    75
  3 | cy   |    90
  4 | dee  |    60
  5 | eli  |    75
```

### A table is a heap, not a list

The SQL standard is blunt: without `ORDER BY`, the order of rows is *implementation
dependent*. The relational model is blunter. A relation is a **set**, and sets have no
order at all. What you just saw is simply the order in which a sequential scan meets the
rows in the table's pages, and on day 1 you saw what an `UPDATE` does to a row: it writes
a new version, somewhere else.

```sql
UPDATE players SET score = 91 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT ctid, * FROM players;
```

```text
 ctid  | id | name | score
-------+----+------+-------
 (0,2) |  2 | bo   |    75
 (0,3) |  3 | cy   |    90
 (0,4) |  4 | dee  |    60
 (0,5) |  5 | eli  |    75
 (0,6) |  1 | ana  |    91
```

`ana` was first. One update later, `ana` is last. Nobody touched the query. The new version
of the row went into the next free slot on the page, `(0,6)`, and the scan meets it there.
On a busy table the same thing happens through updates, deletes, `VACUUM` freeing space
mid-table, and bulk loads, all day long. "Insertion order" holds only until the first
write.

```sql
UPDATE players SET score = 90 WHERE id = 1;
```

parts.title: Ties are unordered too
parts.markdown:
Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day07;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

### ORDER BY with ties is unordered too

This is the version that gets past people who know the first rule. You did write
`ORDER BY`. `ana` and `cy` both have 90:

```sql
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 cy   |    90
 ana  |    90
```

`ORDER BY score` promises an order between different scores. Between equal scores it
promises nothing. Watch what an index does to that "nothing". On a tiny table the planner
would not bother with an index, so for the experiment, discourage sequential scans:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON players (score);
SET enable_seqscan = off;
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2;
RESET enable_seqscan;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 ana  |    90
 cy   |    90
```

Same data, same query, and a different winner. The first plan read the heap and sorted it,
and `cy` came out on top. The second walked the index backwards, and the index stores
equal keys in its own order. On a real table you do not set anything: the planner switches
plans by itself when the statistics change, after an `ANALYZE`, a bit of growth, or a
version upgrade. Your leaderboard changes its mind and nobody deployed anything.

The fix is to make the order **total**. Add a column that is unique as the last sort key,
so no two rows can ever tie:

```sql
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC, id LIMIT 3;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 ana  |    90
 cy   |    90
 bo   |    75
```

And when ties should *share* a place instead of being broken arbitrarily, Postgres 13
added the standard way to say so:

```sql
SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES;
```

```text
 name | score
------+-------
 cy   |    90
 ana  |    90
 bo   |    75
 eli  |    75
```

Asked for three, got four. The third place is a tie between `bo` and `eli`, and
`WITH TIES` refuses to pick one for you.

parts.title: Paging with OFFSET
parts.markdown:
Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day07;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

The textbook way to page through a list:

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  title      text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO posts (created_at, title)
SELECT timestamptz '2026-01-01' + n * interval '1 minute', 'post ' || n
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS n;
CREATE INDEX posts_feed ON posts (created_at DESC, id DESC);
VACUUM ANALYZE posts;

SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3;
```

```text
   id   |    title
--------+-------------
 100000 | post 100000
  99999 | post 99999
  99998 | post 99998
```

That is page 1. While the reader looks at it, somebody publishes a post. Then the reader
clicks "next":

```sql
INSERT INTO posts (created_at, title) VALUES (timestamptz '2026-12-31', 'breaking news');
SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
```

```text
  id   |   title
-------+------------
 99998 | post 99998
 99997 | post 99997
 99996 | post 99996
```

`post 99998` again. `OFFSET 3` means "skip three rows", not "skip the three you saw", and
the new post pushed everything down by one. A delete does the opposite and silently skips a
row. Every infinite-scroll feed built on `OFFSET` has this bug, and on a busy feed it fires
constantly.

### And OFFSET is slow, however good the index

The second problem is cost. `OFFSET` takes a number, and the only thing a database can do
with a number is count. To skip 90,000 rows it has to produce 90,000 rows and throw them
away:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 90000;
```

```text
                               QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Limit (actual rows=10 loops=1)
   ->  Index Scan using posts_feed on posts (actual rows=90010 loops=1)
```

The index scan did its job perfectly, and walked 90,010 entries to hand back 10. Page 9,001
costs nine thousand times what page 1 costs. Users rarely go that deep, but crawlers,
exports and "load all" buttons do.

parts.title: Keyset pagination
parts.markdown:
Starting a new psql session? Run `SET search_path = day07;` first. The tables
are still there, but the setting lasts only for the session.

Instead of remembering *how many* rows you have seen, remember *the last one*. Each page
asks for the rows that come after it in the sort order. With a two-column sort, "after" is
a comparison of the pair, and SQL has exactly that, a **row comparison**:

```sql
SELECT id, title FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-07 22:42:00+00', 10002)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

```text
  id   |   title
-------+------------
 10001 | post 10001
 10000 | post 10000
  9999 | post 9999
```

`(a, b) < (x, y)` means `a < x OR (a = x AND b < y)`, which is "earlier, or at the same
moment with a smaller id". Since the index is on exactly `(created_at, id)`, Postgres can
jump straight to that position:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT id, title FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-07 22:42:00+00', 10002)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

```text
                                                 QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Limit (actual rows=10 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=4
   ->  Index Scan using posts_feed on posts (actual rows=10 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (ROW(created_at, id) < ROW('2026-01-07 22:42:00+00'::timestamp with time zone, 10002))
         Buffers: shared hit=4
```

Ten rows read for ten rows returned. Run the `OFFSET 90000` query with `BUFFERS` added and
compare: whether your numbers say `hit`, `read` or both depends on what is cached, but
their total for the offset version is around a thousand pages, against about four here. A
new post at the top cannot shift this page either, because it is anchored to a row, not to
a count.

Markus Winand, author of *Use The Index, Luke*, has campaigned for years under the banner
"No Offset", and many large public APIs page this way. Stripe's list endpoints take
`starting_after=<object id>` rather than a page number. The trade-off is that
keyset pagination cannot jump to "page 37". It moves forwards and backwards from where you
are. For feeds, timelines, exports and APIs that is exactly what you want. For a search
results page with numbered links, people still use `OFFSET` and accept the cost.

### The keyset that looks right and skips rows

To see why the row comparison matters, take a small feed where two posts share a
timestamp and one was imported late with a backdated time, so `id` and `created_at`
disagree:

```sql
CREATE TABLE feed (id int PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL, title text);
INSERT INTO feed VALUES
  (1, '2026-05-01 10:00+00', 'first'),
  (2, '2026-05-01 10:05+00', 'second'),
  (3, '2026-05-01 10:05+00', 'third'),
  (4, '2026-05-01 10:10+00', 'fourth'),
  (5, '2026-05-01 10:02+00', 'imported late');
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM feed ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 id |       created_at       | title
----+------------------------+--------
  4 | 2026-05-01 10:10:00+00 | fourth
  3 | 2026-05-01 10:05:00+00 | third
```

Page 1 ended at `(10:05, 3)`. The tempting way to write "after that" compares each column
separately:

```sql
SELECT id, title FROM feed
WHERE created_at < '2026-05-01 10:05+00' AND id < 3
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 id | title
----+-------
  1 | first
```

`second` is lost because it shares the timestamp, and `imported late` is lost because its
id is larger. The row comparison gets both:

```sql
SELECT id, title FROM feed
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-05-01 10:05+00', 3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 2;
```

```text
 id |     title
----+---------------
  2 | second
  5 | imported late
```

drill.code:
SELECT name, score
FROM scores
ORDER BY score DESC
FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS WITH TIES;
drill.prompt: Scores: ana 90, bo 80, cy 80, dee 80, eli 70. How many rows does this return?

options.text: 5, WITH TIES returns every row that has a duplicate score
options.why: eli on 70 ties with nobody and comes after the cut, so eli is not included.

options.text: 2: ana and one of the players on 80
options.why: That is plain `LIMIT 2`, and which 80 you get would depend on the plan. WITH TIES exists to avoid exactly that.

options.text: 3: ties count as one row, so ana, bo and cy
options.why: No row is ever merged. The count you ask for decides where the cut falls; WITH TIES then extends the cut past every row equal to the last one.

options.text: 4: ana, then all three players on 80
options.why: The second row is someone on 80, and WITH TIES keeps going while the next row ties with the last one taken. All three 80s share second place, so asking for 2 returns 4. That is the point: it refuses to pick an arbitrary winner among ties.

drill.code:
SELECT id FROM feed
WHERE created_at < '2026-05-01 10:05+00'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 2;
drill.prompt: Page 1 of this feed ended at the post with `created_at = 10:05` and `id = 7`. The rows: (8, 10:09), (7, 10:05), (6, 10:05), (9, 10:01), (5, 10:00). Page 2 should start with id 6. What does this query return instead?

options.text: 9 and 5: post 6 is skipped, because it shares 10:05 with the last row of page 1
options.why: Comparing the timestamp alone with `<` throws away every row at exactly 10:05, including the unseen post 6. With `<=` you would get post 7 again instead. The fix is the row comparison, `(created_at, id) < ('…10:05', 7)`, which returns 6 and 9.

options.text: 7 and 6: the boundary row is repeated
options.why: That would happen with `<=`. Strict `<` excludes everything at 10:05, the seen row and the unseen one alike.

options.text: Nothing: the ORDER BY includes `id`, which the WHERE does not mention
options.why: ORDER BY and WHERE are independent. The query runs without an error and skips a post.

options.text: 6 and 9: the correct next page
options.why: That is what the row comparison returns. This query compares only the timestamp, and 6's timestamp is not strictly less than 10:05.

drill.prompt: `players(id PRIMARY KEY, name, score)`, where two players share the top score. Which queries are guaranteed to return the same row every time?

options.text: None: LIMIT is never deterministic
options.why: LIMIT is perfectly deterministic over a total order. C's order is total because its last key is unique.

options.text: C only
options.why: A has no ORDER BY, so any row may come first: an UPDATE, a plan change or a synchronized scan can change it. B orders by a column that ties at the top, so the winner is unspecified. Only C ends on a unique key, making the order total.

options.text: B and C
options.why: B has a tie exactly where LIMIT cuts. A seq scan plus sort and an index scan can pick different winners for the same data.

options.text: All three, as long as nobody writes to the table
options.why: Even with no writes, A and B depend on the plan, and synchronized scans can start A partway through a large table.

challenges.prompt: The three best players: `name` and `score`, highest score first. Two players tie at the top, so make the answer the same every time by breaking ties on `id`.
challenges.solution: SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC, id LIMIT 3;
challenges.hint: The last sort key has to be unique.

challenges.prompt: The top three by score, but let ties share their place instead of cutting among them: return `name` and `score`, highest first. Use the standard clause for it, not `LIMIT`.
challenges.solution: SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES;
challenges.hint: FETCH FIRST … ROWS …

challenges.prompt: Page 1 of the feed (newest first, ties on `id` descending) ended at the post with `created_at = '2026-05-01 10:05+00'` and `id = 3`. Return the next two posts, as `id` and `title`: compare the pair, not each column on its own.
challenges.solution:
SELECT id, title FROM feed
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-05-01 10:05+00', 3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 2;
challenges.hint: A row comparison: two columns in parentheses on each side of `<`.

quiz.prompt: A query without `ORDER BY` has returned rows in insertion order for months. Name two things that can change that order without the query changing.

options.text: Only a Postgres major-version upgrade
options.why: Upgrades can change plans, but day-to-day writes and statistics changes do it far more often.

options.text: Only a `VACUUM FULL` or `CLUSTER`, which physically rewrites the table
options.why: Those do change it, but so does a single ordinary UPDATE: the updated row's new version lands in the next free slot, at the end of the scan.

options.text: Nothing: Postgres guarantees insertion order for tables with a primary key
options.why: No such guarantee exists. A primary key is an index beside the heap; it does not make the heap ordered, and a sequential scan ignores it entirely.

options.text: An `UPDATE` writing a row's new version elsewhere in the table, and the planner switching to a different plan (an index, a parallel scan, a synchronized scan)
options.why: Without ORDER BY you get whatever order the chosen plan meets the rows in. Writes move rows physically (an updated row is a new version in a new slot) and plan changes alter the path through them. Synchronized scans can even start halfway through a big table. None of it needs a code change.

quiz.prompt: `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 1` on a table where two players share the top score: which one is returned, and how do you make the answer stable?

options.text: The one with the lower primary key, since ties are broken by the key
options.why: Only if you write the key into ORDER BY. Postgres never adds a tiebreaker for you.

options.text: Either: the order among ties is unspecified and can change with the plan; add a unique column as the last sort key, e.g. `ORDER BY score DESC, id`
options.why: ORDER BY only orders rows whose keys differ. A seq scan plus sort and an index scan can return different tied winners for the same data. A unique final key makes the order total. If ties should share the place, use `FETCH FIRST 1 ROW WITH TIES`.

options.text: The one inserted first, because sorting in Postgres is stable
options.why: Whether a sort is stable is an implementation detail, and the input order to the sort is itself not guaranteed. In the lesson an index scan and a seq scan disagreed on exactly this.

options.text: Both: LIMIT 1 returns every row tied for first place
options.why: That is what `FETCH FIRST 1 ROW WITH TIES` does. Plain LIMIT cuts at exactly one row.

quiz.prompt: A feed pages with `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20` for page 2, and a new post is published while the reader is still on page 1. What does the reader see on page 2, and why?

options.text: The last post from page 1 again, because the new post pushed every row down one place and OFFSET skips a count, not the rows already seen
options.why: OFFSET is positional, and inserts and deletes shift positions. An insert above causes a duplicate; a delete above causes a skip. Keyset pagination anchors to the last row seen, so it is immune to both.

options.text: An error, because the result set changed between queries
options.why: Nothing tracks the reader across queries, so there is nothing to detect. That silence is why the bug is so common.

options.text: The new post at the top of page 2
options.why: The new post is newest, so it is at position 1, on page 1, which the reader has already loaded. What page 2 gets is the row that was pushed off page 1.

options.text: Exactly the next 20 posts, because OFFSET is computed against a snapshot of page 1
options.why: Each page is a separate query and sees the data as it is at that moment. No snapshot is held between page loads.

quiz.prompt: Why does `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 90000` stay slow even with an index that matches the `ORDER BY` exactly?

options.text: The rows are sorted in memory before the offset is applied
options.why: With a matching index there is no sort node at all. The time goes into reading and discarding.

options.text: Postgres ignores indexes whenever OFFSET is present
options.why: The plan uses the index: EXPLAIN shows an Index Scan. The cost is the counting, not the access path.

options.text: OFFSET is just a number: the only way to skip 90,000 rows is to produce them in order and throw them away, so the index scan still walks 90,010 entries
options.why: The index gets the rows in the right order cheaply, but it cannot know where the 90,000th one is without counting. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows `actual rows=90010` under a Limit returning 10. Keyset pagination gives the index a value to seek to instead of a count.

options.text: It is fast; OFFSET jumps straight to the right leaf page of the index
options.why: B-tree pages do not know how many entries come before them, so there is no way to jump by position. That is the whole problem.

quiz.prompt: Why must keyset pagination write `(created_at, id) < (x, y)` rather than `created_at < x AND id < y`?

options.text: The AND form is correct but cannot use an index
options.why: It is not correct: it skips rows. Index use is the smaller issue.

options.text: Postgres does not support comparing columns with `AND` in a `WHERE`
options.why: It supports it fine: the query runs and returns the wrong rows, silently.

options.text: The row comparison means "earlier, or at the same time with a smaller id"; the two-condition version drops rows that tie on `created_at` and rows whose `id` does not follow time order
options.why: `(a, b) < (x, y)` is `a < x OR (a = x AND b < y)`. The AND version demands both columns be smaller, which is a different and much stricter condition. It also lets Postgres use an index on exactly (created_at, id) as a single seek.

options.text: They are equivalent; the row form is just shorter
options.why: They agree only while ids happen to increase in time order and no timestamps tie. A backdated import or two posts in the same second breaks the AND form.

quiz.prompt: `SELECT * FROM players` (no `ORDER BY`) lists `ana` first. After `UPDATE players SET score = 91 WHERE id = 1`, the same query lists `ana` last. Why?

options.text: The update wrote a new version of `ana`'s row in the next free slot, and a sequential scan meets rows in the order they sit in the table's pages
options.why: An `UPDATE` never changes a row in place in PostgreSQL; it writes a new version elsewhere (`ctid` shows where). Without `ORDER BY`, the order is simply where the scan finds things.

options.text: `SELECT *` orders by the primary key, and the update changed the key's position
options.why: No order is implied by a primary key. The id did not change; where the row is stored did.

options.text: Updated rows are sorted to the end so the latest change is easy to find
options.why: Nothing sorts anything without `ORDER BY`. The new position is a storage accident, and the next `VACUUM` or update can change it again.

quiz.prompt: Scores are 90, 90, 75, 75, 60. `ORDER BY score DESC FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES` returns four rows. Why?

options.text: It is a bug in older versions; it should return exactly three
options.why: Returning more than three on a tie is what `WITH TIES` is for. `LIMIT 3` is the form that returns exactly three.

options.text: The third place is a tie between the two 75s, and `WITH TIES` keeps every row that ties with the last one rather than picking one
options.why: `LIMIT 3` would cut between the two 75s arbitrarily. `WITH TIES` (PostgreSQL 13) says ties share their place, so the count can come out above 3.

options.text: `FETCH FIRST` counts distinct scores, and there are three: 90, 75, 60
options.why: That would return all five rows. It counts rows, then extends the last place to include its ties.

quiz.prompt: What does keyset pagination remember between pages, and what can it not do that `OFFSET` can?

options.text: A cursor held open on the server; it cannot survive a reconnect
options.why: It holds nothing open: the position is just values the client sends back, like Stripe's `starting_after=<id>`.

options.text: The sort key of the last row it showed; it cannot jump straight to an arbitrary page number such as page 37
options.why: Each page asks for the rows after that position, which an index can find directly and which a new row cannot shift. The price is that "page 37" has no position to start from: fine for feeds, exports and APIs.

options.text: The number of rows already shown; it cannot go backwards
options.why: Remembering a count is what `OFFSET` does, and why it duplicates and skips under writes. Keyset can go backwards by flipping the comparison and the sort.

quiz.prompt: Nobody is writing to the table, yet `SELECT id FROM big LIMIT 3` suddenly returns ids near 100,000 instead of 1, 2, 3. What made it start there?

options.text: A cached plan used an index on `id` backwards
options.why: The plan is a sequential scan both times. What changed is where in the table it began.

options.text: A synchronized sequential scan: another scan of the same big table was partway through, so this one joined it there
options.why: On tables larger than a quarter of `shared_buffers`, a new sequential scan starts where a current one is, wraps round at the end, and they share reads. Turn off `synchronize_seqscans` and it starts at the beginning again.

options.text: `VACUUM` reordered the table by moving old rows to the end
options.why: The rows did not move at all. The same rows were read starting from a different page.

quiz.prompt: Which change makes "the first three rows" of `big` the same on every run, whatever else is happening on the server?

options.text: `ORDER BY id LIMIT 3`
options.why: Only `ORDER BY` promises an order, and `id` is unique so there are no ties to break. With an index on `id` it is also cheap.

options.text: `SET synchronize_seqscans = off` in the application's session
options.why: It removes one cause, not the rule. Updates, `VACUUM` and plan changes can still reorder an unordered result.

options.text: Running `CLUSTER big` once so the rows are stored in id order
options.why: `CLUSTER` sorts the table once; the next updates put rows wherever there is space, and a synchronized scan still starts mid-table.

hooks.remember: Without ORDER BY, row order is whatever the scan meets; an UPDATE alone can change it.
hooks.hook: A query without `ORDER BY` is a **slot machine** that has paid out "insertion order" a thousand times in a row, so everyone thinks it is rigged that way. It is not. One `UPDATE` writes the row's new version into a new slot, the scan meets it last, and the machine pays out something else. **No ORDER BY, no order.**

hooks.remember: ORDER BY says nothing about ties; end it with a unique column, or use FETCH FIRST … WITH TIES.
hooks.hook: Two runners cross the line at 90 points, and `ORDER BY score` has **no photo-finish camera**: a sort might name one winner and an index walk the other. Install the camera, a unique last key (`ORDER BY score DESC, id`), so no two rows can ever tie. Or, when a tie *should* share the podium, `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES` lets everyone on it.

hooks.remember: OFFSET n must read and discard n rows, and shifts when rows are inserted or deleted.
hooks.hook: `OFFSET 90000` is **Sisyphus counting stones**: there is no shortcut to "stone number 90,001", so the database counts every one, then throws them away, on every page load. And if somebody drops a new stone at the front while you are reading, the count shifts by one and page 2 shows you a stone you already saw.

hooks.remember: Keyset pagination remembers the last row and asks for what comes after it: `(created_at, id) < (x, y)`.
hooks.hook: Ariadne did not tell Theseus "turn left 4,812 times". She gave him a **thread tied to where he had been**. Keyset paging is the thread: remember the last row's `(created_at, id)` and ask for what lies beyond it, **as a pair**. Two separate `<` cut the thread: posts sharing the timestamp, or with a larger id, are lost in the labyrinth.

hooks.remember: Synchronized sequential scans let a new scan of a big table start where a running one is, so LIMIT without ORDER BY can begin mid-table.
hooks.hook: A seq scan of a big table is a **train already going round a loop line**. A second query does not wait for a fresh train: it hops on wherever this one is (say, near row 100,000), rides to the end of the line and round to the start. So "the first three rows" are whatever is outside the window when you board.
